en: (B1) Now begins the third quarter.

(Topic 1: Jaimini Sūtra 2.3.1) "But a quality, because of its connection with the sacrifice, should establish a separate rite, since that connection is not subordinate to anything else. (Jaimini Sūtra 2.3.1)

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "If the Soma sacrifice should have the Rathantara as its *sāman*, one should draw the cups beginning with those for Indra and Vāyu; if it has the Bṛhat as its *sāman*, [one should draw] those beginning with the *śukra*.
In this regard, the status of being a condition (*nimittatva*), which is expressed by the word "if" (*yadi*), cannot first of all be construed with either the Rathantara or the Bṛhat.
Because it cannot function as a qualifier for that [referent],
nor can it function as a separate referent (anyapadārtha),
since that lacks the quality of occurring only occasionally.

Nor can it be [an attribute] of the qualified Jyotiṣṭoma; for since other Sāmans are also fixed [in that sacrifice], it is impossible for the Bṛhat and Rathantara to function as qualifiers by excluding association with anything else, and because it is likewise impossible to exclude non-association with them even within the scope delimited by the nature of being a Jyotiṣṭoma.

Therefore, since the meaning of the compound—the state of having *rathantara* as its sole *sāman*—cannot be applied to the archetype ritual (*prakṛta-karma*) as the cause for the precedence of the cups (*grahāgratā*), a distinct ritual qualified by both [the *bṛhat* and *rathantara*] is enjoined;

and as for the word "if" (*yadi*), its meaning is not intended to be significant. This being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), we reply: because the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* are optional in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, their status as qualifiers is possible either by excluding their own non-connection [with the ritual] or by excluding their mutual non-connection.
Nor is it the case that they are absent in every instance delimited by the nature of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*.
This is because [the qualification] is established by being delimited as a praise (*stotra*) following its own intermediate effect;
otherwise, even for you, such [qualification] would necessarily be impossible in the case of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), threshing (*avaghāta*), and so forth, which directly pertain to the sacrifice.
Therefore, it is indeed correct that the sacrifice qualified by the *rathantara* [sāman] constitutes the occasion (*nimitta*).
In reality, however, the sacrifice is not included within the causal factor [of the injunction],
because there is no purpose [for such inclusion]; rather,
by virtue of the status as an auxiliary to the sacrifice understood through the context (*prakaraṇa*), the connection with the other word-meaning is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*).
Otherwise, since the other constituent element—the *jyotiṣṭoma*—is absent in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the precedence of the *śukra* cup and so forth would not apply.

Therefore, even by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the *rathantara* alone is the condition; the specific precedence resulting from that condition is enjoined with reference to the cups that serve as the means for the transcendental result (*apūrva*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*).
Nor is the injunction for the priority of the cup for Indra and Vāyu (aindravāyavāgratva) redundant because it is already obtained through the mere recitation [of the text];
for it is enjoined as a conditional rule (*naimittika*) even prior to that.
And its purpose is the omission [of the rite] in both the archetype (*prakṛti*) and the modified form (*vikṛti*) when the condition (*nimitta*) is absent.

Although in all cases the object of knowledge is merely the necessity of the contingent (naimittika) when the occasioning cause (nimitta) exists, nevertheless, since that [cause] is established here simply by its mention in the text, it should be understood that the object of knowledge is precisely the absence of the contingent when that [cause] is absent.
Therefore, this is not an injunction for a separate ritual act. // 1 // 31 //
Thus ends the second section concerning the Rathantara-sāman.
(B2) [The summary of the subject matter by indicating the reason for not citing the final sentence of the *jagatsāman* passage quoted in the Bhāṣya:

In this Bhāṣya, the passage beginning with “yadi rathantarasāma” and ending with “yadi jagatsāmā āgrayaṇāgrān gṛhṇāti” has been cited. Among these, regarding the *jagatsāman* sentence, because it serves as the proof for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)—namely, that the [new] element cannot be inserted into the archetype sacrifice due to the reason of its connection with the entire ritual (*kratu*)—it is cited.

Since what is mentioned in the Sūtra is impossible because the referent of the word "world" (*jagat*) does not exist, and since it must be established in the tenth [book] that such [a world] cannot be included in the ritual under discussion, the citation of that [Sūtra] would be useless due to the impossibility of its being the final conclusion; with this in mind, he cites the first two sentences alone as being useful for the present inquiry: "The Jyotiṣṭoma... and so forth.
(The meaning of the subject-sentence, the incidental connection with the previous section, and the connection with the chapter:

Those wooden vessels in which the Soma juice is drawn according to the distinction of various deities are called *grahas*; these include the Aindravāyava, Maitrāvaruṇa, Āśvina, and others, which are drawn during the morning libation (*prātaḥsavana*).
In that context, according to the view that the *Rathantara* Sāman is to be used, those *grahas* are to be taken beginning with the Aindravāyava.
In the view that the *bṛhat* is the *sāman*, the meaning of the cited statement is that "those cups are to be drawn beginning with the *śukra*.

In the previous section (*pāda*), it was determined that in both alternative views, since the quality whose status as an injunction is certain cannot possibly apply to the preceding [context], it serves as a differentiator;

whereas in other cases, because it is possible for it to apply to the preceding context—either by being enjoined with respect to the fruit or for the purpose of establishing a restriction—it does not serve as a differentiator.

Now, in order to determine where a quality whose status as the object of injunction (*vidheya*) is doubtful functions as a differentiator due to being enjoined, and where it does not function as such due to the absence of that status, another inquiry is commenced. Without explicitly showing the incidental or topical connection to the chapter— since the determination of difference and non-difference connects it to the chapter— and without showing the lack of immediate connection to the next section because it belongs to a different sub-section, the author states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself, beginning with the word "tatra" (in that case).
(Refutation of the view that the word "yadi" has the sense of a condition:

Although the word "yadi" is seen in such passages as "If one should cause a Rājanya or a Vaiśya to sacrifice," where it functions to express a condition (*nimitta*), nevertheless, in this context, because it is impossible for the qualifier, the qualified, or the qualified whole to constitute the condition, [the word "yadi"] does not function to convey that [condition].
He establishes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) by demonstrating that the quality of superiority based on a specific cause can be enjoined as a subsidiary element of the sacrifice, stating:
"of that which is expressed by the word *yadi*..."
Because it is unfit for functional activity.

In a *bahuvrīhi* compound, since a word such as "rathantara" occurring at the beginning denotes its own meaning as subordinate to the meaning of the other members (*anyapadārtha*), if that [meaning] were connected with the cause provided by another word, the word "rathantara" would become dependent (*sāpekṣa*). Consequently, because of the rule that "there is no formation of a compound for those things that have qualifiers," it would result in the impossibility of forming the compound. Therefore, if the mere "rathantara" alone were the cause, then even when it exists in the fire, [the qualification would apply].
The meaning is that it is improper for the specific form of the *rathantara* to be the condition (*nimitta*), because it would result in its becoming a condition itself;
this is due to the absence of its being merely occasional (*kādācitkatva*).
The meaning of the other word (anyapadārtha) is either the substance *soma* or the sacrifice accomplished by it.

In either case, because there is no occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*), the use of the final member of the *bahuvrīhi* compound would be redundant; furthermore, this would result in the undesirable consequence that the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup and the precedence of the *śukra* cup would be treated as optional alternatives. Therefore, the sense is that the [term *prathamayajña*] does not apply there either.

Since it is impossible for the *kratu* (sacrifice) to be qualified by the *rathantara* [sāman] either through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyāvṛtti*) or the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyāvṛtti*), the view that the cause is a qualified entity does not establish the *rathantara* as the cause.
Nor is it a qualified [cause].

Even on the view that it is a qualified compound (*viśiṣṭa-anvaya*), is the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*) the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or the qualified (*viśeṣya*)? It cannot be the first; for by the rule "in a *bahuvrīhi*, when there is a qualifier, the [word ending in] the seventh case [is placed first]," the word *rathantara* is understood to be the qualifier due to its prior placement, making its status as the qualified impossible, which would result in a violation of established linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*). Nor is it possible for the qualification to occur at the time of the analytical statement (*vigraha*), because the sacrifice—the referent of the other word—is understood as the qualifier by virtue of its being in the genitive case, while the *rathantara* is understood as the qualified by virtue of its being in the nominative case.
This must not be said;

for since the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*) is non-Vedic, it is impossible for the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) contained therein to serve as the basis for the connection with the cause (*nimitta*). Furthermore, since the fact that the *rathantara* is possessed by the sacrifice (*kratumattva*) is already established through the context (*prakaraṇa*) itself regarding the *rathantara* which serves as the cause for the priority of the cups (*grahāgratā*), the qualification of the sacrifice by means of the exclusion of its own non-connection (*svāyogavyāvṛtti*) is redundant.

Since the exclusion [of other sacrifices] from being qualifiers is already established simply because there is no evidence for their inclusion through direct instruction (*upadeśa*), and since such an exclusion would be redundant;

and since even you do not accept the exclusion of others through extended application (*atideśa*); considering the position that the *kratu* (sacrifice) is a qualifier to be illogical, he refutes the second possible position with the words: "The Jyotiṣṭoma...
[etc.].

The meaning is as follows: since there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if one were to enjoin that the *Rathantara* alone is the means [of accomplishment], and since it is untenable to accept an option between two unequal injunctions (*viṣamaśiṣṭavikalpa*), even if that [syntactical split] is not admitted, the status of being a condition (*nimitta*) remains impossible; therefore, the distinction of the ritual action (*karmabheda*) itself is primary.

Furthermore, because other *Sāmans* such as the *Gāyatrī* are specifically enjoined in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* as being connected to other hymns (*stotra*), they are excluded; thus, it is impossible for the *Rathantara* and others to function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) [of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*] when the latter is delimited by the nature of the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself.
This is the sense of the phrase "delimited by the nature of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*" (*jyotiṣṭomatvāvacchedena*).

In cases such as "the conch is white," although it is observed that whiteness functions as a qualifier by excluding its own non-connection with the subject—delimited by the delimitor of the qualificand (viśeṣyatāvacchedaka)—in the present case that is impossible.

The meaning is that in a sacrifice delimited by the performance of other Sāmans such as the Gāyatrī, it is not possible to exclude the non-connection of the Rathantara. Therefore, since the sense of the compound is understood as "this [sacrifice] has the Rathantara alone as its Sāman," and since that [Rathantara] is not established by the context (prakaraṇa) and thus cannot function as a condition (nimitta), it is understood to be something to be enjoined (vidheya).

In the present case of the Jyotiṣṭoma, if the state of having only the *Rathantara* as its *sāman* were enjoined, or if both that and the precedence of the *Aindravāyava* cup were enjoined, a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*) would result. Even if one accepts such a split for the sake of enjoining those [qualities], since the state of having only the *Rathantara* as its *sāman* cannot be directly connected to the Jyotiṣṭoma, it must be understood to find its place through the mantras that serve as the means for the *stotra*. However, in those [mantras], there exists another *sāman*.

Since the injunction is established as distinct, an unequal option (*viṣama-śiṣṭa-vikalpa*) is inadmissible; and because the quality of having *rathantara* alone as its *sāman*—which does not enter into the previous context—is a differentiator, this must be an injunction of a separate ritual action qualified by both [the *rathantara-sāman* and the *agratā*]. In that case, because it is unmanifest (*avyakta*), the *rathantara-sāman* is placed in all the *stotras* obtained through extension (*atideśa*) from the Jyotiṣṭoma; and within that very context, the specific *agratā* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) due to the intermediate context (*avāntara-prakaraṇa*). With this intention, he concludes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).
"From this": [this means] from this.
(An exposition on the justification of the injunction by showing that the word "if" is not intended [to be significant]):

He dispels the objection that the injunctive power of the prescriptive statement beginning with "syāt" (would be) is impaired by the word "yadi" (if), such that it would be impossible for it to enjoin a distinct ritual action, with the words: "But the word 'yadi'..."

The meaning is that since the word *yadi* (if) merely indicates what has already been established by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and since there is no possibility of such establishment [by another means] in this context, the word is devoid of intended meaning—just as in cases such as "the cake for Agni" (*yad āgneya*).

As for the other methods shown in the Vārttika for connecting the word *yadi*, such as: "The abandonment of the word *yadi*, the assumption of an ellipsis (*ruci*) through supply, connection with an intervening element, and the indicative suffix (*liṅ*) expressing cause and effect," and so forth; [these are not required here].
The demonstration of that should be seen in the Kaustubha.
(An investigation [by the proponent] that even the opponent must state that the status of being a qualifier is established only through the mediation of an intermediate effect, etc.):

Even if the status of being a cause, expressed by the word *yadi*, is construed with the qualified object in the form of the sacrifice (*kratu*) as characterized by the *rathantara* chant, the formation of a compound is still possible because there is no obstruction to the semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) defined as "integration into a single meaning" (*ekārthībhāva*). Furthermore, in that context, the application of the *rathantara* chant is restricted to the sacrifice as delimited by the functions of other *sāmans* such as the *gāyatra*.
Since the exclusion of that [other] is established through the attainment [of the specific], the qualification of the *rathantara* is indeed possible;
therefore, intending to show that it is not "non-inclusive" (*aniviśamānatā*), he states the final conclusion: "Of the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*."

The meaning is that, since both [the *ekapṛṣṭha* and the *stotra*] are applicable to the sacrifice through their respective intermediate functions, they serve as qualifiers either by mutual exclusion (*parasparavyāvṛtti*) or by means of their own intermediate effects.
This refers to the phrase "svāvāntara... (their own intermediate...).
Every qualifier must delimit its qualificand through its own intermediate effect (*avāntara-kārya*).

Now, since the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] possess a pervading presence (*vyāpyavṛttitva*) in their intermediate effect, which is the form of the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*, it follows that by means of this, they are indeed mutually exclusive even within the sacrifice (*kratu*), by way of being delimited by their respective delimiters. This is the meaning.
He states the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) for the contrary position: "Otherwise... (*anyathā*).

The meaning is that even for one who maintains that it is a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*), the impossibility of its being characterized by the *rathantara* melody—which is entirely absent in acts such as sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*)—is equally untenable as a qualification (*viśeṣaṇa*).

Although, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), its status as a qualification is due to the exclusion of other melodies obtained through extension (*atideśa*), and not through the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyāvṛtti*);
nevertheless, since the connection with another melody is impossible in the sacrifice itself, the qualification of "having the *rathantara* melody" remains untenable even through that exclusion.

Therefore, since the possession of another *sāman* is obtained for the sacrifice only through the intermediate effect consisting of the form of the hymn (*stotra*), the exclusion must be effected by means of that very [intermediate effect] through the qualification "having the *rathantara-sāman*.
And since this [exclusion] is equal for me as well, it is indicated by the phrase "directly in the sacrifice" (*sākṣād yāge*).

(An explanation of how the *rathantara-sāman* alone constitutes the cause, since the precedence of the *aindravāyava* cup cannot occur in the modified sacrifice due to the absence of the object to be qualified): "Otherwise... [as follows].

The meaning is as follows: although the priority (*agratā*) is prescribed in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the act of drawing the cup (*grahaṇa*), which serves as the means for its own transcendental result (*apūrva*), even when that [priority] is encompassed by the defining characteristic of being a subordinate element in a modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), there is no occurrence of the attainment of that priority in a modified sacrifice that lacks an original injunction (*codaka*), because—just like the offering of that [cup] itself—it lacks the specific occasion (*nimitta*).
(An examination [showing] that since the connection with the qualifier is established by logic itself, even metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is not a fault, etc.):
"Even by means of metaphorical indication."

Although the syntactic connection of the *nimitatva* (causality) with the *rathantara*— which is subordinate to the meaning of another word (*anyapadārtha*)— is unestablished by grammar, nevertheless, when there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the causality— whether it is connected to the qualified whole or to the qualifier— in the verbal cognition due to its lack of occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatvābhāva*),

the injunctions and prohibitions shift to the qualifier according to the maxim "when there is sublation in the qualificand, [the rule] shifts to the qualifier," as in the case of "the crested one has perished" (*śikhī dhvastaḥ*).

Just as in such cases, another argument—namely, that the transfer of the qualification is logically possible—is indicated by the particle *ādi* (and so forth) for the purpose of including what has not been explicitly stated;
likewise, it is indicated that there is no fault in [the word *yadi*] having a secondary meaning (*lakṣaṇā*), rather than assuming that its literal sense is unintended.
Nor is there a lack of purpose in restating the meaning of another word which is obtainable from the context.

In passages such as "the Vairūpa-sāman," because the purpose of restricting the application of the Vairūpa and others to the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* alone—based on their similarity to being designated as *bahuvrīhi* compounds—is stated in the tenth book (*Daśama Adhyāya*), therefore the *Rathantara* alone is the condition (*nimitta*).

And since that [condition] is restricted to the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself, it is therein that the specific *agratā* (priority) is prescribed as a conditional rule (*naimittika*); thus he says: "But the conditional... etc.
(The status of the *bṛhat* that contradicts the *rathantara*, and the *rathantara* that contradicts the *bṛhat*, as the cause [of application] in both the archetype and the ectype.)

Even though only the *rathantara* [sāman] serves as the occasion (*nimitta*), because an injunction (*vidhi*) functions as an impeller of what has not yet occurred, its meaning consists in an occasional duty (*kāryatā*) expressed as "one should act when this exists. Consequently, the connection is with an occasional occasion alone; for the status of being an occasion conveyed by the word "if" (*yadi*) is pervaded by occasionality, and that occasionality is necessitated by the mutual exclusivity of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans].
It should be understood that the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*—the former being opposed to the latter, and the latter being opposed to the former—serve as the respective conditions (*nimitta*).
This opposition arises either because they are optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*) or because one sublates the other (*bādhaka*).

For example, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), due to their optionality, even in the ectype (*vikṛti*), where there is no restriction to one or the other, the precedence of the alternative is omitted due to the absence of the necessary condition.
However, where that rule applies, if there is the presence of another contradictory factor, it [the rule] is set aside because of the existence of a sublation (*bādhaka*).

In that case, although the respective precedence (*agratā*) would be obtained due to the presence of the occasioning factors (*nimitta*) such as the *rathantara*, where—in a sacrificial session (*satra*) and the like—there is no contradiction because both are combined (*samuccaya*), there is an absence of the status of being an occasioning factor; therefore, the meaning is that the respective precedence is simply omitted.
"Simply from the recitation," it says.
This [rule] pertains solely to the priority of the Aindravāyava cup;

however, it should be understood that in the injunction regarding the priority of the Śukra cup, since its acquisition through recitation and so forth lacks the possibility of being already established, the very fact that the contingent duty must necessarily be performed when the occasion arises is what must necessarily be made known.
He concludes the final position with the words: "Therefore..."
(An examination of the purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections:

The purpose in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that another Soma sacrifice, which is a subsidiary of the Jyotiṣṭoma and possesses either the Bṛhat-sāman alone or the Rathantara-sāman alone, must be performed; in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), this is not the case.

Likewise, in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, although the Rathantara-sāman is absent, the sequence beginning with the cup for Indra and Vāyu (Aindravāyava-agra) obtained through the textual recitation is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), while it is not so in the final conclusion (siddhānta); this has not been stated because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the first section concerning the subsidiary status of the precedence of the cups within the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

(B1) (Section 2 / [A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 2]) "In the Aveṣṭi, because of its connection with sacrifice, it is said that the sacrifice is primary" (Jaimini 2.3.3). In the Rājasūya, which has a king as its performer, five sacrifices known as the Aveṣṭi are recorded as separate performances, each with its own prescribed sacrificial fee.

In a sub-section of that [context], it is heard in scripture: "If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, having placed an oblation dedicated to Bṛhaspati in the middle, he should offer oblation after oblation and then pour clarified butter over them; if a Rājanya, [an oblation] to Indra; if a Vaiśya, [an oblation] to the Viśvedevas. There too, as before, the fact of being performed by a Brāhmaṇa and so forth is merely a conditional cause (*nimitta*).

If it is argued that [the term "king"] refers to the Kṣatriya because of the hearing of the word [in the context] of the Rājasūya sacrifice— since that sacrifice is performed by members of the three higher castes and thus accessible to Brāhmaṇas and others as well—

and because the word *rājan* is universally renowned among all people as denoting one who protects the subjects, whereas its usage among the Draviḍas for a mere Kṣatriya is merely a local usage of the Mleccha lands and therefore lacks probative force;
Because [the meaning] is established by grammar, and because that [grammar] is not a restrictive authority as it is rooted in common usage;
and because worldly convention is rooted in the Vedic words *yadi* and so forth.

Therefore, when the agency of Brāhmaṇas and others is the occasion, the performance of a single *iṣṭi* sacrifice consisting of five oblations—characterized by placing [the offering] in the middle and subsequently pouring clarified butter over it—is enjoined as part of the Rājasūya.
It should be understood that there are five individual applications (*prayoga*) corresponding to the five objects in their natural order.

Regarding the statement, "One desiring food should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with this [rite]," since both the obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) applications involve performing the rite outside the *kratu* for the sake of a result, it might be argued that the qualification of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth does not serve as a differentiator. To this, [the sūtra states]: "One should consecrate a king."

Since the Veda prescribes the rite of consecration with reference to one who is already a king, and since the word "king" (rājan) is understood to denote a Kṣatriya even prior to his connection with kingship—which follows only after the qualification for consecration—it is further understood that the word "kingship" (rājya) is preceded by the established usage of the word "king. This is because, under the rule governing the formation of action-nouns (*tasya karma*), the *Smṛti* prescribes the suffix *yak* after the word "king" when it is recited in the *purohitādi* group, according to the rule: "The suffix *yak* is applied after words ending in *pati* and those beginning with *purohita*. Thus, the term *rājya* is known to be derived from the well-established term *rājan*.
According to the usage in the Draviḍa region, the word *rājan* denotes only a Kṣatriya.

Therefore, since Brāhmaṇas and others cannot be the performers [of the Aveṣṭi] in that context, it is understood that they are the objects of the injunction. Consequently, based on the accessory of the agent, a distinct performance of the Aveṣṭi—consisting of a single sacrifice with five oblations and characterized by all its accessories—is enjoined as something external to the [original] kratu.
And by the statement regarding that [sacrifice], food is the fruit.
Within the ritual, there are exactly five applications for each.

Even though, according to both the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), the application of the single *iṣṭi* sacrifice consisting of five oblations is the same;

Nevertheless, the distinction is that in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the quality of being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth does not serve as a differentiator, whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) it does.
And the purpose of this has been stated precisely by demonstrating both positions.

Nor does it follow that, in the sentence concerning the Rājanya, because that [quality] is already established and thus lacks the status of being something to be enjoined, it cannot function as a differentiator; [for it can still serve as such].

Since the term *rājanya* denotes both consecrated and unconsecrated Kṣatriyas, it is logically established that in the Rājasūya sacrifice, this very [term]—being previously unobtained—is prescribed as a differentiator.

For in the Rājasūya, although the word *rāja* has the power to denote Kṣatriyas in general, the eligibility belongs exclusively to consecrated Kṣatriyas due to a conventional (nirūḍha) secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) supported by the indicative mark (*liṅga*) stating, "They call these unconsecrated ones *rājan*.
Therefore, it is proven that in all three sentences, the accessory (*guṇa*) serves to differentiate the performance (*prayoga*).

The word *yadi* (if) serves to indicate the intended meaning—that the two verbal forms constitute a single syntactical unit (*ekavākya*)—insofar as it expresses the sense of "being the cause" (*hetumat*), which is another synonym for "being that which is to be employed" (*prayojyatva*) by the optative suffix (*liṅ*) in the phrase *abhighārayet*.

Therefore, the meaning of the sentence should be understood as: "One should effect the desired result (*iṣṭam bhāvayet*) through sacrifices performed by agents such as Brāhmaṇas, which are the instigators of the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) following the re-offering (*pratyāhuti*) preceded by placing [the butter] in the middle. // 2 //
Thus ends the second section concerning the Aveṣṭi sacrifice.
(B2) [The separate performance of the five Āgneya and other Aveṣṭi sacrifices, and the demonstration that they are specified here as counter-examples:
In the Rājasūya, it is stated: "He offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; gold is the sacrificial fee. To Indra, a cake on eleven potsherds; a bull..."
By the sentences, “The sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) for the Vaiśvadeva is a brown one-year-old cow; the dakṣiṇā for the Maitrāvaruṇī is curdled milk (āmikṣā), a barren cow;
the dakṣiṇā for the Bārhaspatya is a white-backed [bull],” five sacrifices known as the Aveṣṭi are prescribed.

Here, although they share the single name “Aveṣṭi,” just as in the case of the Sākamedha, because the dakṣiṇās are enjoined individually in their respective originative injunctions (utpattivākya), and because of the [distinctive] nature of the dakṣiṇā...

Since the agent is for the sake of the action, and because a difference in agency is perceived through a difference in that [action], and because a difference in performance is understood through that difference,

one must perform each individual ritual act— beginning with the *agnyanvādhāna* and ending with the *brāhmaṇatarpaṇa*— distinctly as qualified by its constituent parts; this is what will be stated in the eleventh book (*adhyāya*), and it refers to those requirements expected by the injunctions of the distinct performances to be enjoined by the sentences under consideration.
He first cites the sentences that prescribe the performance of the preliminary rites: "The Rājasūya," and so forth.
(The refutation of the suspicion regarding another result and the presentation of the proof for the established conclusion:
The term "Rājasūya" is mentioned in order to eliminate the suspicion that there might be another result;
and the phrase "performed by a king" is stated as the proof for the established conclusion.
He cites the scriptural passage that is the subject of the present inquiry: "tadavāntara... etc.
(If "if a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice" is the indication of the subject-sentence, and its meaning is the restatement of the *nidhana* [concluding chant] in the middle of the Vaiśya-sentence:

If a Brāhmaṇa should sacrifice, then, at the time of placing these five oblations on the altar, having placed the Bārhaspatya— which is recited in the fifth position— in the middle, i.e., in the third position, he should place each of the remaining oblations in sequence into the Āhavanīya fire.

Immediately after the pouring [of the oblation], one should perform the sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) over the Bārhaspatya offering—which has been placed in the center—with the remainder of the clarified butter (ājya) remaining in the *juhū* ladle that was used for the under-sprinkling (*upastaraṇa*) and the subsequent sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) intended for the consecration of that oblation; then, at the end, its offering (*homa*) should be performed.
This same procedure is to be understood for the other two offerings as well; such is the meaning of the three illustrative sentences.

In the *Vaiśyavākya*, because the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice is recited in the third position by its very nature, the placement in the middle is obtained through that [recitation] alone; therefore, the injunction for placing it in the middle is a restatement of what is already established (*nityānuvāda*). This distinction was stated in the *Adhikaraṇamālā*:
"The connection with the context [is established] because the agent and other factors differentiate the application (*prayoga*) of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*).

In that regard, qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth differentiate [the action] by way of inducing an injunction, whereas the agent and other such qualities do not connect with the origination of the productive urge (*bhāvanā-utpatti*).

Although it is not possible for that [word] to differentiate [the action] by way of bringing about its injunction, because it is connected with the usage [of the sentence], and since the differentiation of the usage of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) by way of bringing about its injunction is established, [the author], without explicitly showing the contextual connection as it is obvious, states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself:
"In that case also... (*tatrāpi*).
(The prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa] is that, when the Brahmin’s status as the agent is the condition,

there is an injunction of the quality of placing [the offering] in the middle. The meaning is that, since it is logical for the Brahmin’s agency to be connected with the condition expressed by the word "if" (*yadi*), and because this avoids the fault of a complex injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi-gaurava*), there is an injunction of qualities such as placing in the middle within that very sacrifice, when each respective agency is the condition.
He refutes the absence of attainment with the words: "of the Rājasūya."

Now, one might object: since the word "rājā" (king) is heard in the sentence concerning the Rājasūya sacrifice, it is understood that only one possessing the caste-status (*jāti*) denoted by that term—namely, the quality of being a king—is entitled [to perform it]; how then can Brāhmaṇas and others who lack that status obtain eligibility for it? To this, he says:
"of the word 'rājā'... [meaning] "in the sense of one who performs the protection of subjects."

The meaning is as follows: just as words such as *kulāla* (potter), *nāpita* (barber), and *cora* (thief) possess a conventional power (*śakti*) denoting the agency of those respective actions because this is well-known to all the world, so too, since there is no distinction in that regard, the word *rāja* (king) possesses a power denoting the agency of protecting the subjects without being instigated by another. Consequently, because Brāhmaṇas and others are also denotable by that term by virtue of possessing that quality, they obtain the right [to perform the ritual] through that designation.

(Regarding the usage of the word *rājan* even while setting aside the genus [jāti], because the Dravidian usage—even though supported by parsimony (*lāghava*)—is weaker than the aforementioned universal usage: Now, one might object: since it would entail the fault of complexity (*gaurava*) in postulating a delimited adjunct (*sakhaṇḍopādhi*) as the delimitor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), and because the Dravidians use the word *rājan* even for a Kṣatriya who does not protect, it is more reasonable, on account of parsimony, that the word denotes that genus alone. To this, he says: "only a Kṣatriya."

Because the Dravidians are inhabitants of a border region—according to the lexicon, "a border region (*pratyanta*) is a land of barbarians (*mleccha*)"—their usage constitutes a convention established among barbarians. Consequently, like the word *pīlu*, it cannot serve as a proof for the apprehension of a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in the word *rājan*.

For when the deciding factor is already found within the very means of knowledge that apprehends the denotative power, such that no doubt remains, it is not logical for parsimony (*lāghava*), which is inherently not a means of valid cognition, to act as a deciding factor.

Therefore, since the usage of all [words] is determinative even when setting aside the genus (jāti), it is not appropriate here to assume that these words denote a genus, as is the case with words such as *barhis* (sacrificial grass) and *ājya* (clarified butter); this is the meaning.

(An explanation that even grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) serves only to describe correctness and does not serve to apprehend linguistic capacity [*śakti*]): Now, [one might object]—in the sense of "his work" (*tasya karma*), by means of the suffix *ṣyañ* following the word *rājan* as listed in the *brāhmaṇādi* group according to the rule *brāhmaṇādibhyaśca*; or else, because it is listed in the *purohitādi* group, by means of the suffix *yañ* according to the rule *patyantapurohitādibhyo yañ*.

Therefore, since the word *rājan*—whether by means of the suffix *yak* or otherwise—does not convey the sense of "one who performs the protection of subjects" (as is the case with the word *brāhmaṇa*), it is determined through its presentation as an established fact that it denotes a caste (*jāti*) alone. Consequently, because even a weak conventional usage gains strength when supported by the authoritative grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*), it is logical that it denotes only a caste; thus he says: "by grammar... (*vyākaraṇa...*).

Because grammatical tradition (*vyākaraṇasmṛti*) serves merely as an explanatory description of correctness (*sādhutva*), there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing word-potency (*śakti*); or, even if it did, although the word *rājya* is etymologically derived in the sense that "the act of protecting subjects by one who protects subjects is kingship" (*rājyam*), this does not preclude the word *rājan* from denoting the protector of subjects, since that [grammatical tradition] itself is rooted in the linguistic usage of the Dravidians.
The impossibility of [the word *rājya*] being a restrictor [of the denotation] does not follow;
nor, by this much, does the apprehension of the word *rājya*’s expressive power depend upon the apprehension of the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) of the word *rājan*.

For even if it is not understood as the "activity of a king," its status as the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedakatva*) is established precisely when it is understood as the "protection of subjects."
Furthermore, because even universal worldly consensus is supported by such Smṛti texts as, "One should not accept gifts from a king who is not born of the Kṣatriya caste;
one should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a Śūdra," it is not merely on the basis of common consensus that the status of being a Kṣatriya is understood [as the subject of that duty].
By this it is established that the supreme duty of a Kṣatriya alone is the protection of the subjects.
The argument that [the king] is supported by the Smṛtis of Manu and others—such as "The king rules over all, except for the Brāhmaṇa"—is refuted;

for although those texts enjoin the necessity of protection specifically with reference to Kṣatriyas alone, it is possible for one to act as a protector toward Brāhmaṇas and others as well out of personal affection (rāga) and so forth.
Therefore, the meaning is that these texts do not provide support [for the claim that the king has authority over Brāhmaṇas].
On the contrary, he states that the practice of Āryāvarta alone is specifically supported by the Śruti, saying: "sarvaloka... (of all the worlds).

Although there is no difference in the duty of protecting the subjects, and although the Śūdra is excluded due to his lack of the fire and Vedic knowledge established by the injunctions for initiation (*upanayana*) and the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*), the eligibility of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*) for the Rājasūya remains unimpeded; consequently, they are eligible for the *Aveṣṭi* sacrifice included within it, as Brāhmaṇas and the others would otherwise be obtained as performers. Since the status of the King as performer is already established without restriction in the statement regarding the Kṣatriya, the text must therefore be understood as referring to him solely as the occasion (*nimitta*).

Intending that, by virtue of their association with that [preceding case], it is likewise appropriate here for the two sentences concerning the Brāhmaṇas and others to function as causes (*nimitta*), he demonstrates—under the guise of concluding the prima facie argument—the distinction between the occasional (*naimittika*) and the mandatory (*vidheya*) injunctions within that prima facie position, stating: "Therefore... (*ataḥ*).

(Although there is a difference in the formal application (*prayoga*) between the prima facie (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*uttarapakṣa*), this is the determination that, within the *rājasūya*, the single performance consisting of five oblations belongs to the *pūrvapakṣa*:

This is the meaning: here, it is not merely the act of sprinkling (*abhighāraṇa*) that is enjoined as a contingent (*naimittika*) rule; for it would be impossible to treat the mention of "placing in the middle" as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Therefore, since the special sprinkling (abhighāraṇa) qualified by "placing in the middle" is untenable without the performance of a single iṣṭi consisting of five oblations, and because it cannot be included in the performances of single-oblation iṣṭis, the sprinkling qualified by that characteristic of "placing in the middle"— by virtue of the force of that qualification— necessitates a distinct performance. Consequently, although the necessity of necessitating a distinct performance is equal for both the prima facie and the final views, under the view that [the rule] serves as a condition (nimitta), the performance of the single iṣṭi with five oblations is an occasional (naimittika) rite even when occurring within the Rājasūya.
It is established.

However, on the view that [the injunction] is prescriptive (*vidhāyaka*), one must consider the difference in purpose (*prayojana-bheda*) in that such a distinct performance (*prayogāntara*) occurs entirely outside of the Rājasūya. Now, in response to the expectation—"Where, then, under the view that [the injunction] has a conditional purpose (*nimittārthatva*), do the individual performances included within the Rājasūya find their place?"—he says: "individually" (*pratyeka*).

The meaning is as follows: although for those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) there is an absence of the caste belonging to their respective fathers, the presence of the caste belonging to their respective mothers is stated in the various *smṛtis*. Consequently, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Kṣatriya mother possesses the caste of a Rājanya; thus, he has the entitlement (*adhikāra*) to perform the Rājasūya sacrifice, and the individual performances pertain to him. However, if it is considered that even for such a person, by the sentence "if [he sacrifices] a Rājanya," only the performance of a single *iṣṭi* consisting of five oblations is obtained, and therefore the individual performances do not find a place, then [the following applies].

In that case, since there is no possibility of sublation due to the lack of occasion for even the individual applications, it should be understood—indicated by the word "bodhyam" (it should be known)—that these [individual rites] are also to be performed in combination by their respective performers.
(By the statement "one desiring food and drink should sacrifice with this," both applications are enjoined for the sake of an external result.

Now, an objection: if this is so, does not the injunction "one desiring food and drink should sacrifice with this" entail yet another application for the sake of food and drink? To this, he says: "etayā" (with this).

And in this sentence, since there is no other quality associated with the application that would give rise to a distinction [between the rites], and because when a performer is required, the expectancy is satisfied by the Kṣatriya who is the performer of the *Aveṣṭi* mentioned in the *Rājasūya* sentence— precisely because he is the one immediately present— it is logical for him to be construed as the performer; thus, since the quality associated with the application exists, only a further application (*viniyoga*) of the *Aveṣṭi* alone is effected.

And thus, since simultaneous performance is impossible for the production of multiple results according to the principle of the section on the accomplishment of yoga (Yogasiddhyadhikaraṇa), the meaning is that even externally, those respective performances must be carried out for the sake of food and other such ends.

(An introduction to the conclusion: that even by virtue of the authority of the Dravidian tradition, which is supported by Śruti and Smṛti, it is established that only one possessing the [specific] caste is intended here.

Although both traditions are equal in their status as supporting factors for the Smṛti, he establishes the conclusion by demonstrating that the Dravidian tradition is more trustworthy in its authority because it is supported by the Śruti, the foremost of all means of valid cognition—[as expressed in the verse] beginning with "the king."
The meaning is that, indeed, in the case of consecration (abhiṣeka), it is to be performed solely as the means for accomplishing the authority to protect [the realm].

Now, since the word *rājya* is taught [by Pāṇini] as ending in the suffix *yak*, it is necessary to first determine the meaning of its base, *rājan*; furthermore, because it is well-known among the Dravidians, he states that it is also supported by traditional authority (*smṛti*) in the words:
"The action pertaining to that."
(An examination of why the form ending in *ya* is more appropriate, in order to justify the Vedic hearing of the acute accent on the vowel of the suffixal *ā* in the word *rājyāya*):

Although here the derivation of the word *rājya* is identical whether by means of the suffix *ṣyañ* or *ya*, nevertheless, even in the absence of any distinction in common usage, it is said: "They are consecrated for the sake of sovereignty (*rājyāya*"); they call these consecrated ones 'kings' (*rājānaḥ*)."

In such scriptural passages as these, since the vowel *ā* contained within the suffix of the word *rājya* is observed to have the acute (*udātta*) accent, it is logical that the word ends in the suffix *yak*. For then, while the term *anta* (end) from the rule “The end of a word ending in *ghañ* preceded by *karṣa* or *ātvat* is acute” is being carried over, and the term *taddhitasya* (of a secondary derivative) is also being carried over, the rule *kitaḥ* prescribes acuteness for the vowel *ā* of the suffix *yak* by treating it as if it were the beginning or the end of a single unit, according to the principle “in a single element, [the beginning and end] are treated as one. Thus, it is established that the word ends in *yak*.

The status of being udātta (acute-accented) by virtue of the suffix is obtained. However, if the form were derived from the suffix *ṣyañ*, then by the rule *ñnityādir nityam*, the initial syllable would be prescribed as udātta; consequently, the vowel *r* of the base (*prakṛti*) would retain its udātta accent.
With this conclusion established in the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding the determination that the suffix is *yaṅ*, [the author] has presented the sūtra simply as *patyantapurohitādibhyaḥ*.
[The prescription of another performance by agents such as Brāhmaṇas, etc., and the determination of its performance outside the sacrifice, etc. is found in the scriptural statement itself.
Thus, the application of the term *Āryāvarta* is indicated by the word "only" (*eva*) to be figurative (*gauṇa*), based on its association with the quality of performing royal duties.

Consequently, since Brāhmaṇas and others are not already established as agents [of the sacrifice], they cannot serve as mere conditions (*nimitta*); therefore, they must necessarily be enjoined. Since enjoining multiple qualities—such as the agency of Brāhmaṇas and others—in reference to a sacrifice already established would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), [the agency of Brāhmaṇas and others] does not fit into the preceding [context]. Thus, from this form of agency belonging to Brāhmaṇas and others which was not previously included...
Intending to show that there is a difference in application based on the quality, the author of the Siddhānta indicates the thing to be enjoined with the words "ataśca" (and therefore).

Furthermore, with reference to the fact that another performance (prayoga) is established by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) grasping its own subject as being outside the *rājasūya*, the term "outside the sacrifice" (*bahiḥkratu*) was used.

Consequently, the meaning is that the performances of the *aveṣṭi*—which are uninterrupted from the hearing of the [words] "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth—are indeed distinct [from the main sacrifice], yet remain included within the *rājasūya*.

When there is a requirement for a result regarding this very other performance to be executed outside the sacrifice, the connection with the result is established by the sentence "One desiring food should perform this [sacrifice]" (*etayānnādyakāmaḥ*), since it obtains the status of an injunction for what is required.
But it does not apply to that which is included within the Rājasūya;

for since that [Rājasūya] has no further expectancy once its fruit of sovereignty (svārājya) is attained, it would follow that it could not be the object of an injunction for something not already required. With this intention, he says: "And of that... (tasya ca).

By this, the following [objection] is also refuted: that because the mention of food (*annādya*) occurs by referring to the subject at hand (*prakṛta*) through the word *etad* (this) and taking only the *iṣṭi* as the basis, the *iṣṭi*— having its requirement satisfied by the inclusion of food which allows no other scope— does not accept the fruit of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), which has scope only in a domain distinct from that.

Since the performance [of the *annādya* sacrifice] by a Brāhmaṇa also has its own scope, one must conclude that the individual performances of the *iṣṭi*s consisting of single oblations are for the sake of *svārājya*, in order to justify their inclusion within the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Rājasūya. With this intention, he says: "within the sacrifice" (*antaḥkratu*).

By this [statement], the following is meant: although each individual sacrifice and the group of five sacrifices consist of single oblations, and thus both types of performance are included within the great ritual complex (*mahāprayoga*) of the Rājasūya, the opponent’s claim that both yield the fruit of food (*annādya*) is incorrect.

For even though there is no difference in their proximity (*sannidhāna*), it is improper to establish a connection with something that lacks a mutual requirement (*anākāṅkṣita*). Therefore, the logical conclusion is that only the other performances—those performed by Brāhmaṇas and others—are fit to yield that specific fruit.
(The purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections:
That is the purpose.

The meaning is that this is made clear by demonstrating two positions: in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), although there is a difference between the performance of the *aveṣṭi*—which is part of the *rājasūya* sacrifice—and the performance performed by Brāhmaṇas and others, since both aim at self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), it is also performed for the sake of food (*annādya*);

whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), there is a separate performance solely for the sake of food, while those for the sake of self-sovereignty are indeed distinct. Thus, the two positions are established.

(Regarding the statement concerning the Rājanya: the doubt that the sacrifice consisting of five oblations performed by a Rājanya as a restatement of the term "Rājanya" is for the sake of the fruit of self-sovereignty (*svārājya*), and thus should be performed within the sacrificial session. Now, even if those [sacrifices] are enjoined in the statements concerning the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya, since the King is already established in the Rājasūya in the statement concerning the Rājanya, he is not something to be enjoined; and although, because he is permanently established, he cannot serve as a conditional cause (*nimitta*), the word "if" (*yadi*)—just as in the statements concerning the Brāhmaṇa and the Vaiśya—[indicates a condition].

Anticipating the objection that—since it is possible for the reference to the Kṣatriya (*rājanya*) to be merely reiterative by means of the act of renunciation (*parityāga*) and so forth, and since the "placing in the middle" (*madhyenidhāna*) cannot be included within the performance of the five sacrifices (*pañceṣṭi*), it must therefore enjoin a different performance; yet even so, because that [performance] can be carried out either optionally or cumulatively as part of the *Rājasūya* for the sake of the fruit of sovereignty (*svārājya*), there is no resulting necessity for its performance outside [the *Rājasūya*]—he raises the doubt with the words: "And not... (*na ca*).

He offers a rebuttal with the words "of the term *rājanya*," intending that its purpose is established as follows: since it would be redundant for the term *rājanya* to be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and since it denotes all Kṣatriyas—both those who have been consecrated (*abhiṣikta*) and those who have not—it follows that a non-consecrated Kṣatriya is not already established in the Rājasūya and must therefore be enjoined. Consequently, following the logic of the passage concerning Brāhmaṇas and others, this is justified by enjoining a distinct performance based on the status of being a Kṣatriya in general, in relation to the performance included within the Rājasūya for which a consecrated person is the qualified agent. Thus he replies: "of the term *rājanya*."
How is it that only one who has been consecrated [as a king] has the entitlement [to perform] the Rājasūya?
To this he says: "For in the Rājasūya... [and so on].
This refers to the *nirūḍhalakṣaṇā* (established metaphorical indication).

Furthermore, regarding its capacity to convey meaning (*śaktigrāhakatva*), it cannot be considered a conveyor of primary denotation (*śakti*) because, if one were to postulate a power based on the possession of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by consecration (*abhiṣeka*), there would result the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) in the determinant of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*).

Rather, since the genus *kṣatriyatva* (the state of being a Kṣatriya) is simpler, it merely serves to grasp the intention (*tātparya*) through a conventional metaphorical indication (*nirūḍhalakṣaṇā*) of that which possesses the primary power.
For this very reason, in the context of the Rājasūya sacrifice, the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) states: "He indeed becomes a lord of the quarters who establishes the quarters," and so forth.

The meaning is that since the designation of "lordship" (īśvaratva) is impossible for a mere Kṣatriya without the removal of thorns [from the earth] and the protection of subjects— and since only one who has been consecrated has the authority (adhikāra) for that task— one must take the term in its figurative sense (lākṣaṇika-artha).
This has been stated by way of elaboration.

(Regarding the statement that although the term *rājanya* is a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it refers to one who has been consecrated, the performance for the sake of food and wealth occurs outside the sacrifice—this is the presentation of the final conclusion [siddhānta]: In reality, however, since the verb *yajati* from the sentences concerning the Brāhmaṇas and others is supplied here by ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*), and because a distinction in performance is established both to avoid inconsistency (*avairūpya*) and by the force of the injunction of the accessory (*guṇavidhi*) consisting of placing [the vessel] in the middle, that [performance] is connected with the sentence regarding food and wealth; thus, one who desires food and wealth [should perform it].
Although the term *rājanya* is a restatement (*anuvāda*)— since the consecrated performer acts for the sake of food and drink as understood from sentences such as "the Indra [cup] in the middle"—

nevertheless, according to the principle of the *yogasiddhi-adhikaraṇa*, even if self-sovereignty (*svārājya*) arises from the performance of other Rājasūya rites, the fruit of food and drink does not arise; therefore, an external performance (*bahiḥprayoga*) is indeed justified in accordance with that [requirement for the specific fruit].
In the Vārttika as well, this very position has been adopted;
the rest is clear.
Since the purpose is evident from the presentation of both positions, it has not been stated explicitly.

And just as in these two positions, although there is no attainment [of the *dakṣiṇās*] when they are combined into a single performance because each of the *dakṣiṇās* is restricted to a single individual performance, nevertheless the attainment of the *dakṣiṇās* occurs; this will be explained in the eleventh [book].
Thus ends the second section concerning the *Aveṣṭi*.

(B1) (3rd Adhikaraṇa / [A.2 Pāda 3 Adhi.3]) Regarding the *Ādhāna* (the laying of the sacred fires): "Because it is subsidiary to all. Jaimini 2.3.4 states: "In spring, a Brāhmaṇa should lay the fires; in summer, a Rājanya; in autumn, a Vaiśya"—thus it is heard in the Śruti.
Likewise, there is the injunction: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in spring, a Kṣatriya in summer, and a Vaiśya in autumn.

In that context, since the sacrifices common to all social classes (*varṇas*) are to be accomplished through fire and knowledge, and since the establishment of the fire (*ādhāna*), which serves as the means for that fire, is enjoined by the rule "He who, knowing thus, establishes the fire"—which prescribes the establishment with reference to the fire itself and possesses a potency not restricted to any other purpose—[the initiation must be performed by all].

Since the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) is already established for Brāhmaṇas and others by other means, its mention here serves the purpose of indicating a specific occasion (*nimitta*).
That is, when the agency of a Brāhmaṇa is the occasion, the spring season is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *ādhāna*.

Alternatively, the statement "then he collects the materials" (*atha saṃbhārān saṃbharati*), which is a supplement to another injunction, may be a mere descriptive reference (*vartamānāpadeśatā*) rather than an injunction itself.
Nevertheless, the injunction "one establishes the fire on the preparatory materials" (*saṃbhāreṣv agnim ādadhāti*) is an injunction that brings about the act of establishment (*ādhāna*).
For here, the preparatory materials themselves are not the object of the injunction, as they are already established by other means of knowledge;
nor is the status of being their locus the object of the injunction.
Since this [fire] is already established by the very wording of the mantra, "Let him place this in it," this [passage] is merely an injunction for the act of placing (ādhāna) itself.

Alternatively, it is an injunction regarding the time, referring back to the placement already established, for the purpose of the middle voice (*ātmanepada*), which signifies that one who has not performed the placement does not possess the Āhavanīya fire.

And it cannot be an injunction [for the fire-installation], because that would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). The statement, "One who has a son and has black hair should install the fires," is the injunction that establishes the installation of the fires (*ādhāna*).

However, in the aforementioned sentence, by virtue of its being directed toward prosperity (*abhyudaya*), the injunction regarding the status of the substratum (*adhikaraṇatva*) arises from the wording of the mantra itself even prior [to the general injunction].
And thus, in the sentence concerning one who has a son, there is no need to resort to an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a specific stage of life (*vayo'vasthāviśeṣa*).

In every respect, since the entitlement [to the rites] is obtained through the act of laying the fires (*ādhāna*), the scriptural mentions of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth serve merely as indicative marks (*nimitta*) and are not causes for differentiation.
Likewise, study is implied as a means for acquiring knowledge (*vidyā*), and initiation (*upanayana*) is implied as a means for that study;

furthermore, for study itself, there is a restrictive rule (*niyama*) established by the injunction "one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) is to be studied. Therefore, with reference to the initiation which is obtained as common to all [classes], and with the condition (*nimitta*) of being performed by a Brāhmaṇa, [the time] is "spring" (*vasanta*).

When it is argued that "the time [of the rite] is being prescribed," we reply: since, just as there is the possibility of all [classes] being agents, there is also the possibility of all times being applicable to the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) and other rites, there is no decisive reason (*vinigamanā*) to determine whether the injunction is for the time with the Brāhmaṇa agent as the condition, or for the agent with the time as the condition; therefore, it is simply an injunction for the *ādhāna* and so forth as qualified by both [the Brāhmaṇa agent and the specific time].

Furthermore, since the initiation (*upanayana*) is already established as a possibility under certain circumstances, its prescription is all the more justified. Precisely for this reason, because there is no decisive factor [to the contrary], and since qualities such as the agent or time— which are connected to the performance— necessarily entail a prescriptive injunction regarding the performance itself,

the injunctions concerning age and stage found in sentences such as "when a son is born" (*jātaputra*) are merely restatements (*anuvāda*) of the performance prescribed by that primary injunction, serving to enjoin an agent qualified by a specific age and stage.

Furthermore, because a subordinate element (guṇa) connected with origination and so forth is heard as the object of the middle-voice ending (ātmanepada), origination and the rest must also pertain to this very [act],
and not to the sentence concerning one whose son has been born;
for that would result in a split of the sentence (vākyabheda).
Alternatively, because of its primacy, origination and the rest pertain only to the Brāhmaṇa statement, while in the other two there is merely application;
thus, even here, a difference in application is established on account of the accessory.

Although these two—the *ādhāna* (consecration of the fires) and the *upanayana* (initiation)—have as their fruit the acquisition of the sacred fires (*agni*) and knowledge (*vidyā*), they are also obligatory (*nitya*), because it is heard in scripture that there is sin (*pratyavāya*) from their non-performance.

And thus, when the acquisition of the sacred fires and knowledge has been obtained through the *ādhāna* and *upanayana* prompted by their own respective injunctions, the injunctions for the sacrifices (*kratu-vidhi*) do not prompt the fires or the knowledge, nor their means; therefore, the purpose—that one devoid of them, such as a *śūdra*, lacks eligibility—is what will be stated in the sixth [book]. // 3 //
Thus ends the third section concerning the application of one's own ritual rules, beginning with the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*).

(B2) Since it is established by this very logic that the *upanayana* (initiation) also lacks being prompted by its own injunction, the purpose of the prima facie argument—that there is eligibility for Śūdras in ritual acts—is rendered possible. Regarding the prima facie view that the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) is not prompted by its own injunction, the purpose [of the discussion] is to refute the impossibility of Śūdra eligibility for rituals on the grounds of their lack of learning; for, since a Śūdra has not undergone initiation (*upanayana*), they do not engage in study, and thus, due to ignorance, cannot be eligible for ritual acts. Therefore, just like the sentences concerning the *ādhāna*, the injunctive sentences concerning the *upanayana* must also [be considered].
He cites [the following examples] together, even though they are not explicitly mentioned in the Sūtra, as subjects for investigation: "In spring," etc.

Furthermore, since the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is not enjoined even in the sentences concerning initiation according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is possible for the requirement of learning to be fulfilled by the injunctions of ritual acts (*karmavidhi*)—just as it is for the three higher castes—even in the case of a Śūdra. Therefore, the sense is that his eligibility (*adhikāra*) arises from that very source, and thus there is no obstacle to the stated purpose.

(An exposition on the connection with the preceding chapter and section [pādādhyāyasaṃgati], the connection by way of a counter-example [pratyudāharaṇasaṃgati], or the connection by extension [atideśikasaṃgati], etc. In the final position (siddhānta), because the establishment of the sacred fires (ādhāna) is distinct from its accessories by virtue of the injunctions for its own respective sentences, whereas in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) there is no such distinction due to the absence of an injunction, the connections with the chapter and section are established; just as in the case of the Aveṣṭi sacrifice, since Brāhmaṇas and others cannot serve as the occasion (nimitta) for it due to the absence of their eligibility [to perform it].

Although a difference in application might arise from its being subject to injunction, since the possibility of its attainment exists here, let it be for the sake of a condition (*nimitta*); thus, because the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) arises in this manner, [the author] proceeds by way of a counter-example. Alternatively, just as in the previous case a doubt regarding its being for the sake of a condition was raised and refuted to establish that it is an injunction, so too here; and thus, without explicitly showing the extended application (*atideśika*) connection or the doubt, as they are clear.
He states the prima facie position (pūrvapakṣa) itself with the words: "In that regard" (tatra).
(The sacrificial injunctions are to be accomplished through the knowledge of fire):
Because the qualification belongs to anyone who merely desires heaven, and because the desire for heaven is possible for all social classes (*varṇa*), it is said "all classes.
This is because [the rites] are to be accomplished through the knowledge of fire.
The meaning is as follows: since the Āhavanīya fire and others are enjoined as subsidiary elements by injunctions such as "one offers in the Āhavanīya," they are accomplished by means of the fire;
and since recitation is impossible without the study [of the Veda], it is accomplished by means of knowledge (vidyā).

(An objection regarding the impossibility of implying the *ādhāna*— the rite of establishing the sacred fires— which employs the non-worldly *āhavanīya* fire, even when there is an implication of *vidyā*, because the causal relationship between the injunction for ritual action (*kratu*) and the study and knowledge (*adhyayana-vidyā*) is established by worldly experience: "Now, although it is possible for the injunctions for rituals to imply [the study] because the world establishes that study produces knowledge and thus understands it to be a means [to that end], how can the injunctions for rituals imply the *ādhāna*— which is not a constituent part (*anaṅga*) [of the sacrifice]— given that the status of the *āhavanīya* as a means [to the sacrifice] in its form of an unseen potency (*adṛṣṭa*) is not known from any other source?"
To the objection that [the fire] would be cast upward, he says: "And of the fire."

The phrase "not implied by anything else" (*ananyākṣipta*) is stated in order to avoid the lack of a definitive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) as to whether the injunction for the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) applies here or in the sentences concerning the Brāhmaṇas and others.
The meaning is that, because there is no other thing to be enjoined here, the injunction pertains to the fire-installation itself;

whereas in the sentences concerning the Brāhmaṇas and others, since it is possible to enjoin qualities such as springtime (*vasanta*), it is not appropriate to resort to an injunction of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

And thus, since even the restatement of "one who knows thus" (*vidvān*) is justified by the very knowledge implied by the injunction for the sacrifice, the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*), which is understood as a means through the sentence concerning the knower, is itself implied by the injunctions for the sacrifices; and since that [laying of the fires] is established as common to all four castes, the mention of "Brāhmaṇa" and so forth serves the purpose of indicating a specific occasion (*nimitta*).

(When the agency of a Brāhmaṇa is the occasion [nimitta], there is an injunction regarding time, characterized by a substratum that follows the positive and negative concomitance with the occasion for the sake of the mere establishment of the sacred fires.
Nor is it impossible to understand the status of being an occasion in the absence of the word *yadi*;

for since that which is established in its own form is fit to connect precisely as an occasion, its connection in that capacity is justified even in the absence of the word *yadi*. With this intention, he says: "The hearing [of the text] is for the purpose of indicating the occasion."
He shows what is to be established: "in the case of being performed by Brāhmaṇas."

The phrase "as an auxiliary to the *ādhāna*" (ādhānāṅgatvena) is stated to indicate that since the *ādhāna* is already established by the very production of the fires (*agnyutpatti*), and thus only the *ādhāna* itself is the object of reference (*uddeśya*), there is no occurrence of the fault of restating a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭānuvāda*).
This also serves as an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the *upanayana*.
Consequently, the meaning is that a restriction regarding the spring season and other times as the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*) is enjoined with reference to that [the *ādhāna*].

Therefore, although time cannot be considered "occasional" (*naimittika*) in the sense that its performance depends on a specific occasion— such as the *sandhyāvandana* and other rites— it should nevertheless be understood as such by virtue of its being the substratum that conforms to the presence and absence of those occasions.

(Explanation of why the fire-installation (*ādhāna*) is common to all, despite the fact that both the installation and the initiation (*upanayana*) are intended objects [of the injunction]): Although both the fire-installation and the initiation are intended objects (*uddeśya*) characterized as being desired (*īpsitatva*), there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because the intended objects are not of diverse classes (*vijātīya*). Nor is there such a split even though time is an intended object—since it cannot be something to be enjoined (*vidheya*)—because it is indeed subject to being enjoined.

And thus, since the Brāhmaṇas and others are excluded from other times, it is established that Śūdras and others, who are distinct from the Brāhmaṇas and so forth, have no fixed time [for such actions]; this is the intended meaning.
(An examination of the alternative view that [the mention of] time and occasion serves as a restrictive injunction regarding the performers, such as Brāhmaṇas, etc.):
Here, "the spring season" is an *upalakṣaṇa* (an indicative mark).

This is because, through the injunctions for sacrifices (*kratu*), there arises the possibility of implying the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) as common to all social classes (*varṇa*).

For even if the *ādhāna* (the rite of establishing the sacred fires) were implied [as a prerequisite], it would not be implied as something occurring within the performance of the sacrifice (*kratu-prayoga*), because the fires are prescribed for disposal at the end [of the sacrifice]—just like the sacrificial vessels—and thus cannot be considered common [to all rites]; consequently, they are understood to be performed outside the performance at an unrestricted time. However, in the case of the *upanayana* (initiation), since its purpose is study (*adhyayana*), its exclusion from the performance [of the sacrifice] follows by its very nature (*sāmarthya*).

Therefore, since the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and the initiation (*upanayana*)—which would otherwise occur at indefinite times because they must precede the *agnihotra* and other rites—are restricted to specific seasons such as spring, it is possible to enjoin the restriction of their performers to Brāhmaṇas and others.

And on this view, it is established that even for the establishment of the fires performed at times other than spring, such as winter, there is no restriction regarding Brāhmaṇas and other castes as performers.
In every respect, there is no injunction of the establishment of the fires qualified by both [season and caste] in the sentences concerning Brāhmaṇas and others.
It should be understood that this is because [the teaching] is received out of reverence and because it is possible to obtain it from other sources.

(Since the statement "one who knows thus" cannot serve as an injunction for the fire-laying (*ādhāna*) because it functions as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) for the preparatory materials (*saṃbhāra*), one must follow an alternative view that the injunction for the fire-laying is found in the text: "he places the fire in the preparatory materials.

Because the sentence concerning the "knower" contains the relative pronoun *yat* and is a description of a present state (*vartamānāpadeśa*), it is impossible for it to be an injunction for the fire-laying; therefore, due to this lack of conviction, he states an alternative view with the words "or else."

The mention of being a supplement to another injunction (*vidhyantaraśeṣatva*) is introduced in order to dispel the suspicion that this [text] is an injunction (*vidhi*) by virtue of its being composed in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood. For this statement—accompanied by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating, "It overcomes the rival and the enemy"—is a general rule (*sāmānya-vidhi*) regarding the materials such as water and so forth, which are prescribed by specific injunctions such as "he pours out water," under the heading: "Now he collects the materials."

The procedure for its establishment (sthāpana) is the remainder [of the injunction]. Since the praise of the establishment is made through an explanatory statement (arthavāda)— to the effect that "the wise man who, having first performed the establishment of water and so forth, establishes the fire in this manner, shall, by the power of the subsidiary element consisting of the act of establishment, deprive even a powerful enemy of his livelihood"— it is understood as being supplementary to the injunction.
The meaning is that it is injunctive by virtue of the assumption of the *leṭ* [Vedic subjunctive] mood.
"By another means of knowledge" (*pramāṇāntara*)... [etc.].
The meaning is that the materials consisting of wood and earth are already established by other scriptural statements.

Furthermore, this indicates the rejection—by the author of the *Nyāyasudhā*—of the view that the injunction here is merely for the act of establishing the fires (*ādhāna*), because it would be qualified by the status of being the locus for the materials (*saṃbhāra*).

For if that were the case, the same logic would apply to the sentences concerning the crocodile and so forth, resulting in the contingency of a qualified injunction for the establishment of the fires in those cases as well; thus, there would be no basis for determining which one is the primary injunction.

Therefore, since there is no other thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) here, and because the injunction for the act of laying the fires (*ādhāna*) must necessarily be accepted in this very context, this is simply the injunction for the pure laying of the fires (*śuddhādhāna-vidhi*).

Furthermore, because no accessory (*guṇa*) or the like connected to the performance (*prayoga*) is heard therein, and because the performance is already established by the primary injunctions themselves—just as in the case of the *prayāja* offerings—it is not enjoined at all;

rather, following the statements regarding the accessories (*guṇavākya*), it is merely the production (*karaṇa*) of the application (*viniyoga*) directed toward fire in general, which is synonymous with "one who has laid the fires" (*āhitāgni*). Thus, the meaning is that the injunction of springtime (*vasantādividhi*) is indeed a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the laying of the fires, being prompted by the injunctions for the sacrifices (*kratu-vidhi*).
(An alternative view is followed: that even for the one who performs the fire-consecration, the injunction for the consecration is established by another statement that brings it about;
thus, it is an injunction regarding the time.)
The phrase "in the sentences concerning spring, etc. is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the context].
