Because the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is not specified in the sentence regarding the *saṃbhāra* offerings, it is not understood that the status of being the *āhavanīya* fire is absent for one who has not established the sacred fires (*anādhātṛ*).

Since it is possible for the *āhavanīya* status to accrue sequentially to another person even from fires established by someone else, there is no prior application (*aprāpti*) of the *āhavanīya* status connected solely to the establisher (*ādhātṛ*), which would serve to exclude others; therefore, in the sentences concerning spring, etc. [the injunction is indeed restrictive].
The meaning is that because its injunction would be mandatory, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

However, in the case of the *jātaputra* passage, since the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) is heard, when an injunction for the fire-laying (*ādheya*) qualified by that purpose has been stated, one might ask: "What, then, is enjoined in the *saṃbhāra* passage?

In response to this expectation, it is accepted that the injunction regarding the *saṃbhāras* being the locus for that [fire-laying]—which is inferred from the wording of the mantra, "In that [fire], let it be laid"—precedes [the injunction of the *jātaputra* passage].

He provides the answer: "In the stated sentence, however, it is precisely the status of being the basis for the equipment that is enjoined, for the sake of making [the practice] the pinnacle of prosperity. This is expressed in the words: "But in the stated sentence... and so forth.

If the sentences beginning with "In spring" were injunctions for the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration), then, since the *ādhāna* is already established by other means, enjoining the two qualities of having a son born and having black hair would result in a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). In the Siddhānta, as in the case of the rule "half within the altar" (*ardham antarvedi*), the words "having a son born" and "having black hair" would have to undergo an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of age; however, he shows that this does not apply here because the *ādhāna* qualified by these [qualities] is enjoined right here, which constitutes a parsimony of effort (*lāghava*)—thus [he says]: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

Because the locative case is non-determinative due to the absence of distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and the like, and because there is a lack of a deciding factor (*vinigamanāviraha*) between an injunction regarding time and an injunction regarding the agent, the Vasantavākya enjoines the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*) as a qualified act.
This is what is meant by "due to the lack of a deciding factor."
Nor should it be said that the locative case alone is the regulator [of the meaning];
for in the absence of repetition (*vīpsā*) and the like, we do not observe the locative following a word denoting time to convey that [meaning].
Otherwise, there would be the consequence of the redundancy of employing the repetition in the phrase *vasante vasante jyotiṣā*.

Furthermore, since the term *brāhmaṇa* cannot logically be the object of reference (*uddeśya*) due to its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb form whose meaning denotes the agent (*kartṛvācya*), it follows that neither [the agent nor the caste] can serve as the causal condition (*nimitta*). Therefore, the meaning is that it is logical only to regard this as an injunction for the installation of the fires qualified by both [the agent and the caste].
(On the necessity of restrictive injunctions in the formula for the initiation ceremony) "all the more so" means: //

The meaning is as follows: although the injunctions for ritual acts (*kratu-vidhi*) necessarily imply knowledge [of their procedure], the study (*adhyayana*) that is the means to that knowledge is not necessarily implied by them, because such knowledge can be obtained through other means even without those injunctions. Furthermore, since study is possible even for one who has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), the initiation (*upanayana*), which is the means to that study, cannot be necessarily implied either. Therefore, since initiation might only occur optionally (*pakṣe prāpta*), an injunction of necessity (*niyamavidhi*) is all the more required for it.
(Exclusion of the Śūdra from eligibility on the grounds that the *ādhāna* and *upanayana* are prompted by their own injunctions):

If it is accepted that the sentences concerning spring (*vasanta*) and so forth pertain solely to the origination (*utpatti*) and application (*viniyoga*) [of the rites], then there would result a lack of connection for the factors associated with performance—such as the agent, time, and so forth—since it would be necessary to hold that the performance itself is what is enjoined right here [in these sentences]. Consequently, the *ādhāna* and *upanayana* must indeed be understood as being prompted by their own respective injunctions.

Considering the parsimony [of postulation]— namely, that since the injunctions for sacrifices are already obtained, one need not assume them to be the motivators (*prayojaka*), and since the entitlement (*adhikāra*) is already established for the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), one need not assume the status of the *śūdra* as entitled nor assume that these injunctions necessitate the means for obtaining fire and knowledge— one should understand that what is to be enjoined in the sentences concerning spring and so forth, under the guise of establishing the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vidhi*), is actually to be enjoined even by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sentence regarding "having a son born."
He demonstrates this with the words "for this very reason."
Arising and so forth also occur in this very [context].

And therefore, just as there is a difference in the ritual application (*prayoga*), the meaning is that there is also a difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the fire-installation (*ādhāna*).

(The determination that the fire-altar (*agni*) and sacred knowledge (*vidyā*) are obligatory because of scriptural declarations regarding the sin incurred by their non-performance when enjoined by their own specific injunctions, and not because they are implied by the injunctions for obligatory sacrifices):

Nor should it be argued that—even though the fire-altar and sacred knowledge are enjoined by their own respective injunctions—their performance would not necessarily follow due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) indicating their obligatoriness; therefore, it is necessary that they be implied by the injunctions for obligatory sacrifices. This is because... [text truncated]

Even though it is established that the injunctions for obligatory sacrifices depend on fire and knowledge provided by others for the sake of brevity, there is no proof that a sin arises for one who lacks them when they do not perform those sacrifices, even if such a sin does arise for one who possesses the fire and knowledge established by their own respective injunctions; therefore, it is illogical for these injunctions to imply [the necessity of] them.

By this, the argument of Pārthasārathi—that because the sacrifice-injunctions are obligatory, the injunctions for the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*) and so forth are also obligatory as a matter of fact—is refuted.
Intending to set aside [the objection] with the words "apāstam" (it is refuted), he establishes the eternality of those two in another way, beginning with "etayośca" (and of these two).

The meaning is that these two [study and the fire-laying] are obligatory (nitya), because the scriptures declare sin (pratyavāya) for the non-performance of study, knowledge, and initiation through such passages as: "Those who do not study become outcasts (vrātyas)"; "This man is a mere pillar; he is a mere bearer of burdens who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning"; and "The time for initiation for the Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, and Vaiśya has passed; beyond this, they fall. Furthermore, since the scripture states, "One should not die without having established the sacred fires," and the state of being one who has not established the fires is listed among the minor sins (upapātaka), it is understood that there is sin in the non-performance of the fire-laying ceremony. Thus, both are obligatory.

(Regarding the meaningfulness of the *apaśūdra* section as being intended for the purpose of this present section: He removes the charge of redundancy against the *apaśūdra* section with the words "And thus" (*evañca*).

The meaning is that the section concerning those who are not Śūdras (*apaśūdrādhikaraṇa*) is intended to state the purpose of what has been established here—that these sentences regarding spring and so forth constitute injunctions for the laying of the fires (*ādhāna*).
Thus ends the third section concerning the application of one's own rules for the establishment of the sacred fires and so forth.
(B1) (Section 4 / A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 4) In the case of sacrifices, there is a separate injunction because of the connection with a specific name. Jaimini 2.3.5:
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is heard in scripture: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Dākṣāyaṇayajña."

Likewise, it is heard in scripture: "One desiring cattle should sacrifice with the Sākaṃprasthāyīya. Since this is not well-known in common worldly usage, it is understood to be a name (nāmadheya), like the word *udbhid* and others. Consequently, either by virtue of its designation (*saṃjñā*) or due to the repetition of the injunctive suffix (*abhyāsa*), a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*) is enjoined;

for since the connection with the fruit is already established by the statement that all desires may be attained through sacrifices (*sārvakāmyavākya*), there is no other purpose [for this injunction]. This being the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), [the reply is: although the accessory (*guṇa*) is not well-known in common usage;

Nevertheless, since the term *dākṣāyaṇa*—derived from the analysis "the sacrifice whose performance (*ayana*) consists of the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of that [sacrifice] performed by these *dakṣas*, who are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) of the sacrificer Dakṣa"—is understood to have repetition as its primary meaning;

and since the term *sākaṃprasthāpya*—derived from the analysis "that in which there is a departure together (*saha-prasthāna*)"—is understood to have simultaneity (*sahatva*) as its primary meaning, it is not determined to be a name (proper noun) by assuming an additional power [of denotation]. Therefore, the qualities consisting of repetition and simultaneity, which were not previously established, are enjoined with reference to the fruit.

When the question arises as to how many times there is a repetition, because of the specific injunction in the sentence, "One should sacrifice at two full-moon days and two new-moon days," there is indeed a double repetition.

Furthermore, when the question arises as to by what means there is simultaneity (*sahatva*) in the departure, because of the statement, "He should step forward together with the two *kumbhī* vessels," [the simultaneity] is by means of the two *kumbhīs*.

And by this very statement, which prescribes that stepping forward is the substratum of simultaneity, the status of being its substratum is established even in the absence of an intermediate context (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*).
However, due to the context (*prakaraṇa*), the basis [of the injunction] is indeed the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).

Therefore, since there is no status as a proper name (*saṃjñātva*) here, and because there is no repetition (*abhyāsa*)—as it is intended to establish a connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a result (*phala*)—there is no separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).

In fact, however, according to the traditional rule (*smṛti*) "the suffix *ṇa* occurs after a preceding word when forming a name," the suffix *ṇa* would not apply to the word *dākṣāyaṇa* if it lacked the status of a name. Thus, [the term is established as a name].

Even though the conventional meaning (saṃjñā) is necessarily present, because the term is accepted as having both etymological and conventional meanings (yogarūḍhi) through the cognition of the meaning of its constituent parts, the exclusion of the form of the etymological meaning—which has not yet been established—is enjoined for the sake of the result;
thus, there is no contradiction. // 4 //
Thus ends the fourth section concerning the Dākṣāyaṇa sacrifice.
(B2) (The citation of the *sākaṃprasthāyīya* passage is for the purpose of establishing the validity of the plural number in the word "ayaneṣu"):

Although the word "ayaneṣu" in the Sūtra indicates that the passage concerning the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* is the example being cited, [the author] cites the passage concerning the *Sākaṃprasthāyīya* together as well, because it follows the same logical principle as suggested by the use of the plural number— namely, the passage beginning with "darśapūrṇamāsayoḥ."
(The purpose of stating "of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices"):

In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the phrase "of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices" is stated for the sake of identifying the counter-correlate to the difference between acts; and in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is stated for the sake of identifying the connection with the quality consisting of repetition.
(The determination of the connection with the subsequent chapter and section.)
(The prima facie view regarding the term *dākṣāyaṇayajña* as a name:

The meaning is that [the word] is not established either through the conventional usage of the whole or through the conventional usage of its parts;

"Of Dakṣa."

As for the statement in the *Kaustubha* that the mention of plurality is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to characterize duality, that is incorrect because there is also an injunction for an alternative procedure: "the milking process in the evening, the milking process in the morning.
Thus, since the two pots are used together during the *abhikramaṇa*, there is no contradiction, as that [mention of plurality] was intended with reference to that.

Thus, since holding [the ladle] below the *sruc* and the cutting of the *iḍā* portion have been prohibited up to that point, it follows by logical fitness (*yogyatā*) that giving it to another is obtained; therefore, the giving to the *agnīdh* priest, which is already established as his duty (*karmakaratva*), is restated.

And in this way, even though there is no intermediate context (*antar-prakaraṇa*) regarding the vessels (*prastha*), the connection with the *kumbhī* as the locus of the collective action and its status as the substratum (*āśrayatva*) is established—this is the meaning.
(Admission that [the term] is a name for a *dākṣāyaṇa* in order to justify the initial *ṇatva* of the first member)
— thus, by the Smṛti.

And since, by this [rule], the substitution of *ṇ* for the cause (the preceding word) excluding the letter *g* is prescribed only when [the word] is a technical name (*saṃjñā*), it follows that in the absence of being a technical name, that substitution would not occur; therefore, the meaning is that its status as a technical name is necessary.

The purpose of the preceding and following sections is as follows: according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the performance of the *Dākṣāyaṇayajña* and other such rites occurs outside the application of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), just as in the case of the *Saurya-iṣṭi* and similar offerings.

According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, these are performed through the repetition of the New and Full Moon sacrifices themselves; this has not been stated explicitly because it is self-evident.

By means of these two [injunctions], "One should sacrifice the *iṣis*" and "He pours out four handfuls," which enjoin the touching of the *iṣis* and the pouring out of four handfuls belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), there is a restatement (*anuvāda*) by means of the two [injunctions] taught as unattached (*anārabhyādhīta*)—
namely, "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu" and "One desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should pour out a sacrificial pap (*caru*) to Sūrya."
The two qualities, whiteness and the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), are prescribed:
the sacrificial animal (*iṣā*) that serves as the object of the act of taking hold must be made white,
and the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) must be performed in a vessel indicated by the word *caru*.
And the statement that [the offering] belongs to Vāyu because of its connection with the wind among all trees is a restatement (anuvāda);
likewise, the term "saurya" refers to the [offering] belonging to Agni alone,
due to the commonality of having fire as their deity.
But it is not an injunction regarding a deity, because no sacrifice is heard [in the text].
In both cases, the mention of the fruit is a restatement (anuvāda) of the fruit already established by the "Sārvakāmya" passage; this is the first position.

The second [view], however, is that because it would result in the redundancy of the word expressing the fruit (*phala*), and because a connection between a quality (*guṇa*) and a fruit is untenable due to the lack of a contextual substrate (*āśraya*), a distinct ritual act—consisting of the touching (*ālambhana*) and offering (*nirvāpa*) as previously mentioned and qualified by the quality—is enjoined for the sake of the fruit. But the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is as follows: since it would otherwise lead to the redundancy of words ending in *taddhita* suffixes such as "dedicated to Vāyu" (*vāyavya*) or "dedicated to Sūrya" (*saurya*), [the injunction] is inferred from the relationship between the substance and the deity.
The sacrifice itself—characterized by its verbal root and distinguished by the substance and deity—is enjoined with reference to a specific result;
as for the acts of touching (*ālabhati*) and pouring out (*nirvapati*), they are not enjoined since they are already obtained through extension (*atideśa*). // 5 //
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the distinctness of sacrifices involving specific materials and deities.
(B2) [The determination of the connection, etc.

Here, because there is an investigation into whether the quality characterized as a deity—which has an unascertained status as that which is to be enjoined—is a differentiator, there is a connection with the chapter and the section; likewise, because it serves as a refutation of the mere injunction of a quality after restating the meaning of the verbal root as stated in the preceding section, there is an immediate connection by way of refutation (*āpavādikī*).

And because it is clear, [the author] does not state it explicitly, but rather states the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) preceded by a specification of the subject matter: "One should sacrifice a tawny animal."
The meaning of the term *riṣāpada* is a specific piece of wood, long like the shaft of a plow, which is fixed upon a cart.
(Regarding the acceptance of the two sentences concerning Vāyu and Sūrya as injunctions of accessory qualities for the sake of parsimony:

Since it is improper to assume a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) when an injunction of an accessory quality (*guṇavidhi*) is possible—and since it is improper to assume a sacrifice that is not explicitly mentioned in the text—he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that these are merely injunctions of accessories: "of those two enjoined by these [two sentences]," meaning "without reference to a specific context" (*anārabhya*).
The meaning is that because the *kañcana* sacrifice is not mentioned within the context of a specific ritual (*prakṛti*), it is "taught independently" (*anārabhyādhīta*).

He provides the justification for the interpretation by accepting that the word *śvetam* refers to the sacrificial post (*iṣākāṣṭha*) and that the accusative case in *carum* functions as a locative (*saptamy-arthe lakṣaṇā*), stating: "having become the object of the act of touching."

If it is argued that, because of the exclusion of the *śūrpa* (winnowing basket) by the primary scriptural injunction, the prescription of the *sthālī* (pot) as the locus [of the offering] is impossible, then—in view of the fact that the term *caru* indicates a specific measure—one must understand the first prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) to be a prescription that the *sthālī* is the measure denoted by the word *caru*; for even the accusative case is justified as a qualifier of the action, such that the handfuls of grain to be poured out (*muṣṭinirvāpa*) should be made so as to result in a quantity measured by a *caru*. Thus, the *caru* should be prepared in such a way that the grains become measured by a *caru*. This is how the prescription of the *sthālī* as the measure denoted by the word *caru* is to be seen in the first prima facie position.

(The presentation of the second prima facie view [pūrvapakṣa]: "An intermediate action, distinguished by its qualities, is enjoined with reference to a fruit, as that which is to be refuted by the third sūtra.
In this regard, as a reply to that prima facie view, it is stated:
"Or rather, [the injunction applies] to the extent that has been mentioned, because the action is rooted in the Vedic revelation" (Jaimini 2.3.13).

Having thus applied the first sūtra, [the author] intends that the third sūtra—which establishes the final position (*siddhānta*)—should also be applied by repeating it as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). With this in mind, beginning two investigations simultaneously (*tantra*), he sets forth the second prima facie argument: "But the sacrifice [belongs to the sacrificer], because of the connection with the enjoyer of the fruit of the substance, due to these [persons'] connection with the ritual action" (Jaimini 2.3.14). He explains the second prima facie view.
"But the second [alternative]" refers to the consequence that the word "result" (*phala*) would be rendered meaningless.

In the world as well, since the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices alone are invariably present due to their connection with the [rites of] "taking hold" (*ālambhana*) and "extinguishing" (*nirvāpa*), this also indicates the absence of any evidence for [the application of the rule] to other sacrifices.

(An examination of how the term *nirvapati* serves to establish the similarity with the archetype for the two sentences concerning Vāyu and Sūrya, even though they [otherwise] characterize a sacrifice:
"The substance and the deity...")

Since the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix denotes a deity who is the recipient of the oblation (*havirbhāk*), and since such a deity is necessarily constituted by a sacrifice, there arises an expectation for a sacrifice.

Because that sacrifice is not established by any other means of knowledge, it must be enjoined by this very sentence. Between the requirement of supplying an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) and the use of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the latter is the simpler course; therefore, the sacrifice is indicated by each respective verbal root.
The meaning of the word *śakya* (capable/possible), however, is restated because it has already been established by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, the purpose of employing words with their technical definitions (*lākṣaṇika*) is to establish a similarity of form (*prakṛtisādṛśya*) consisting in the connection with a sentence containing verbal roots such as *nirvapati* (he offers).

For this very reason, the injunction “one should sacrifice in an enclosed space” (*pariśrite yājayed*), which is recited in the context of the archetype (*prakṛti*) alongside the text “one should offer a *caru* oblation to Soma and Rudra,” is of the same class as that [archetype].

In a sentence whose primary purpose is to enjoin the quality of being "enclosed" (pariśrita), even the indicative mark (*liṅga*) consisting of a reference to the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is compatible with the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of a sacrifice within the act of "offering" (*nirvapati*).
The intended meaning is that the term *pariśrita* refers to the encircling of two [objects] with materials such as mats at the time of the principal rite.

As for the connection with the enjoyer of the fruit mentioned in the Sūtra as a means of inferring the sacrifice, that is intended merely to indicate the rejection of the status of being a preparatory rite (*saṃskārakarma*) proposed by the first prima facie opponent; thus, there is no fault.
Thus ends the fifth section concerning the distinctness of sacrifices involving specific materials and deities.

(The explanation that the touching of the calf alone is intended, because there is no possibility of touching [the cow] due to the separation from the calf known as the *vatsopāvasarjana*, and because the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "beloved by the calf" is thus justified):
A sacrifice is not postulated merely on the basis of a connection with a substance in the case of the *ālabhati* [rite], but rather on the basis of a connection between a substance and a deity.

Just as in the case of the passage "and he lets go the calf," where, due to the connection with the accusative case, the injunction is for letting go with reference to the calf, so too here, because it occurs in a section primarily consisting of injunctions for purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), the meaning is that the injunction for touching is intended precisely as a purificatory rite for the calf.
Nor should it be argued that the injunction is untenable because the act of touching— known as *ālambha*— is already implied by the very act of letting go.

This is because, in the rite known as *dhenu-viyoga* (the separation of the cow), there is no mandatory requirement for the Adhvaryu priest to touch the cow while keeping her near him; thus, [the touching by another] is logically consistent.

For this very reason, even though the touching is performed by the Adhvaryu, there is no inconsistency in the milking being performed by someone else. Consequently, in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating "animals are indeed fond of their calves," since it is declared that animals are dear to their calves, the mother is one who is beloved by her calf.

Thinking that the justification for the praise—"it will flow with affection because of the son's flattering words, or because of the affection being aroused by those flattering words"—is possible only if [the root] denotes mere touching, he says: "of the root *ā-labh*.
(In this section, the connection between the *pāda* and the *adhyāya* is established.)

In this established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it should be observed in the *Kaustubha* that the connection between the [specific] section and chapter is justified because this touching (*ālambha*)— unlike the touchings belonging to the New and Full Moon sacrifices— is a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) due to the quality of the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) being non-prescriptive (*anupādeya-guṇa*) and due to the difference of context (*prakaraṇāntara*). In the passage from the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa* regarding the fire-altar, "He places the *caru* [oblation]; for nīvāra grains are indeed the food of Bṛhaspati," one might ask: how can the food of the sacrificer be the food of Bṛhaspati?

This is because, even if Bṛhaspati were not explicitly the deity, his status as the deity is understood through the sense of the passage; furthermore, in the Taittirīya recension, there is a supplementary statement containing a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) word: "It belongs to Bṛhaspati" (*bārhaspatyo bhavati*).
Therefore, this is indeed an injunction prescribing a sacrifice inferred from the relationship between the material and the deity.

Since that [rice-offering] consists of medicinal substances (*oṣadhadravyaka*), the *sviṣṭakṛt* and other rites of disposal (*pratipatti*) would apply to it by extension from the *Āgneya* sacrifice. In response to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that the injunction “he places the *caru* down” (*carum upadadhāti*) prescribes this placing down as a rite of disposal, [the following is said]: although there is the hearing of a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) in the Taittirīya recension, nevertheless, because there is no independent injunction and because it would result in breaking the syntactic unity with another injunction, this is not a secondary derivative suffix denoting a deity (*devatātaddhita*).

Furthermore, because the injunction "he places the *caru*" prescribes the placement as a consecratory act (*saṃskāra*) for the *caru* that produces the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), there is no requirement for a deity; thus, one cannot postulate an injunction regarding a deity even one inferred from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
For this very reason, one must postulate an injunction for the very raw material required by the *caru*, namely the *nīvāra* grain itself.

Consequently, since the praise "the *nīvāra* grains are the food of Bṛhaspati, the Brāhmaṇa" is thus rendered possible, it is established that the phrase "or of Bṛhaspati" does not, by way of postulating a deity, imply the existence of a sacrifice. // 7 //
Thus concludes the seventh section, concerning the fact that the *naivāra* porridge is for the purpose of the *ādhāna*.

(B2) (An investigation into the connection between the preceding and subsequent sections and their subject matter): Here, the connection between this section and the previous one (*pādādhyāya-saṅgati*) arises because, in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is a distinction between the productive energy (*bhāvanā*) of separate sacrifices caused by the quality of the deity whose status as an object of injunction is certain, and the productive energy of the act of disposal (*pratipatti-bhāvanā*) consisting of the placing [of the bricks]; whereas in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), such a distinction does not exist. Furthermore, while in the preceding case the assumption of a sacrifice was impossible due to the non-hearing of a deity, here, because a deity is indeed present, the assumption of a sacrifice is certainly possible.

Since the immediate connection—consisting of a counter-example by way of extension (*atideśa*) arising from the presentation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)—is clear, it is not explicitly stated; rather, the author states the *pūrvapakṣa* itself, preceded by an example, beginning with the words "In the fire" (*agnau*).

Although it is recorded in the Kaustubha that, after stating, "The sacrificial porridge is made of nīvāra rice; for nīvāra is the food of Bṛhaspati," the text "he places the porridge" is heard [in the scripture], nevertheless, this sequence of sentences has been written here in accordance with the Śāstradīpikā, because even if written out of order, the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) regarding its purpose being for sacrifice remains tenable.

(An exposition according to another recension [śākhā] that the dedication to the deity is performed by means of the mantra "Of Bṛhaspati"): In that regard, first, in the sentence concerning the *naivāra* [rice-offering], once the productive urge (*bhāvanā*)— which has the *naivāra* rice as its instrument— is implied and enjoined by an injunction because it was previously unestablished,
the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) stands in need of a purpose, and the productive urge stands in need of a verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*) to serve as its delimiting factor.

Even though the postulation of some meaning for the verbal root is necessary, since the placing (*upadhāna*)—being a refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the *caru* by virtue of the accusative case—is incapable of being the instrument (*karaṇa*) therein, its status as a delimiting factor (*avacchedakatva*) is untenable. Therefore, intending that the sacrifice itself must be postulated as the delimiting factor on account of the sense and the capacity of the *caru* substance, he refutes the doubt regarding the absence of a deity when the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is to be established, stating: "It is the food of the sacrificer."

The meaning is as follows: because the genitive case in the word *bṛhaspateḥ* indicates a relationship with the wild rice (*nīvāra*), and since no other relationship is possible, it must be accepted that the relationship is precisely that of being the deity (*devatātva*). Furthermore, since this [relationship] is untenable without a sacrifice, the nature of the sacrifice is determined. He states—*bārhaspatyo bhavati*—to show that the fact that this specific relationship, namely the state of being the deity, is intended is also understood through the supplementation (*upasaṃhāra*) of the passage found in another recensional branch (*śākhā*).

The meaning is as follows: since it has been determined that the word *bārhaspatya*—which stands in grammatical apposition with the previously mentioned word *caru* in the passage “This sacrificial porridge (*caru*) is indeed directly food”—is a derivative formed with a suffix denoting a deity (*devatā-taddhita*), it is understood here as well that the genitive case [in *bārhaspatyasya*] refers to the status of being a deity, because it possesses the same referent as that [word].
(An exposition on the establishment of the *pratipatti* [disposal] of the *caru*): What, then, is enjoined by the sentence concerning the *upadhāna*?

In response to this inquiry, since this sacrifice belongs to the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the fire-altar (*agni*), and because of its similarity in having medicinal herbs (*oṣadha*) as its substance, the *upadhāna* is enjoined as the *pratipatti*, thereby setting aside any other disposal that would have been obtained through extension (*atideśa*).
And thus, the meaning is that the distinction between the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of sacrifice and the productive activity of disposal (*pratipatti*) is established.
This very point he states with the words: "And of that... (*tasya ca*).
(The determination that *bārhaspatya* is not a *devatātaddhita* suffix, but rather a *prāgdīvyatīya* suffix:
For in all cases, only a meaning required by an injunction is enjoined by an injunction inferred from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), and never one that is not required.

Thus, here in the case of "he places the *caru*," because the injunction for placing [the vessel] as a means of purifying the *caru* would otherwise be logically untenable, [it implies] the *adhvaryu*...

Just as in the case of [the injunction] "he chooses," since the application of the *caru* is conceived as being for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), the mental realization (*bhāvanā*) having the *caru* as its object is already established through the very fact that [the preparation] would otherwise be inexplicable;

and because a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*) is not accepted in the sentence concerning the *naivāra* [offering], when there is a requirement for a material substance (*prakṛtidravya*) for the *caru*, the mere prescription of *nīvāra* as its material is sufficient. Since a deity is not required in that context, one cannot postulate an injunction for a deity inferred from an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).

Intending that it is appropriate to assume the status of an injunction for the statement "The [oblation] belongs to Bṛhaspati" by imagining it to be a prescriptive rule, and thus to assume its purpose lies in that injunction, he states the final position (siddhānta) with the words: "Even though...
and "the taddhita suffix denoting a deity."
Furthermore, it is a *taddhita* suffix *ṇya* prescribed in the sense of "pertaining to" (*prāgdīvyatīya*) [as per Pāṇini 4.1.83]; this is the remainder [of the argument].

[This concludes] the determination that, even in the absence of a conceptualization of a sacrifice, there is indeed an injunction for a *caru* characterized by the act of placing [the potsherds], [and that it serves] as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the *caru*.

By this, the statement of the *Prakāśakāra*— that because the production of the sacrificial ground (*sthala*) is already occupied by the Vedic bricks (*śrauteṣṭakā*), it is impossible for the sacrifice to be postulated (since the accomplishment of the *caru* prescribed by the assumed injunction would be untenable), and therefore the piling (*upadhāna*) serves solely that purpose— is refuted; [for the grounds for such a conclusion do not hold].

In the case of the *caru* (gruel), the *kumbhī* (pot), the bricks, and so forth—among these four—the removal of the central bricks for the purpose of placing [the *caru*], their replacement, and the filling [of the space] are prescribed for the sake of establishing those specific bricks; thus, there is no contradiction with the bricks. Even under the view that this is a primary act (*arthakarma*), since the incidental production of the ground-space is necessary, the contradiction with the bricks remains unavoidable.
The intended meaning is that there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the sublation of the second sense.
(The justification for the *arthavāda* is that since the word *bṛhaspati* denotes a Brāhmaṇa, its connection [to the *naivāra* offering] is solely for the purpose of praising it;

for the word *bṛhat*—in accordance with the meaning of the root *bṛh*—denotes the Veda, just like the word *brahman*, and the word *pati* denotes a protector, and because of the scriptural statement: "Having performed austerity, he created the Brahman [Veda] and the Brāhmaṇas for the protection of the Veda.")

Because of the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*) that [Bṛhaspati] is the protector of the Vedas, the word *bṛhaspati* is understood to denote a Brāhmaṇa; and because of the Smṛti rule— "The food of a sage is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa"— which praises the wild *nīvāra* grain (the food of forest-dwelling sages) as fit for a Brāhmaṇa’s *śrāddha*, the status of being "belonging to Bṛhaspati" (*bārhaspatyatva*) mentioned in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) refers to its connection with Brāhmaṇas, and is intended for the purpose of praising the *nīvāra*.
However, intending to show the justification for the explanatory passage (arthavāda) on the grounds that [the deity] is Bṛhaspati, he says: "And therefore... (ataśca).

Even though, in the Taittirīya [Brāhmaṇa], the word *bṛhaspati* might refer specifically to Bṛhaspati—the priest of the gods—on account of the etymological derivation (*yogarūpa*) found in the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) stating “Brahman indeed is the priest of the gods,” and not to a Brāhmaṇa by mere etymology alone;

nevertheless, since the praise of the *nīvāra* grains is established even through that mere connection, the assumption of a deity is not supported by any valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). This is the intended meaning.

And therefore, considering that there is no separate productive activity (*bhāvanā*) of a sacrifice apart from the productive activity of the placing (*upadhāna*), he concludes: "Thus it is established."
Thus ends the seventh section concerning the purpose of preparing the sacrificial porridge.
(B1) (Section 8 / [A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 8]) But in the case of the *pātnīvata*, there is a restriction because of its prior mention. Jaimini 2.3.19:

Having enjoined a sacrifice characterized by a specific substance and deity with the words, "They should immolate the *tvaṣṭṛ*-related *pātnīvata* animal," it is further heard in scripture: "They release the *pātnīvata* after it has been encircled by fire."

In this regard, since it is impossible to refer to the first sacrifice dedicated to both deities by means of the term *pātnīvata* alone— just as one cannot refer to the *āgneya* sacrifice by saying "one divides the *āgneya* into four parts"—

and since the subsidiary element of *paryagnikaraṇa* (the act of carrying fire around) would be obtained through extension (*atideśa*) even if it were to be enjoined, and because enjoining a restriction (*parisaṅkhyā*) on other subsidiaries would result in the three-fold fault (*traidoṣya*),

the established position (*siddhānta*) is that the word *paryagnikṛta* is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*), and this is therefore an injunction for a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*). Thus it was argued.
Because of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), it is not a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).
Nor is there any impossibility of it being a restatement (*anuvāda*);

for even though Tvaṣṭṛ and Patnīvat possess a devatā-hood that functions as a composite whole (*vyāsajyavṛtti*)—just like Agni and Soma—it is possible to denote them through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), just as the word "Agni" is used in the *manotā* hymn.
In reality, however, because the secondary derivative suffix (taddhita) is heard separately, these are indeed two distinct deities;
yet, because they are included within a single sentence, there is a conjunction (samuccaya).
Therefore, just as one can say "the mother of Ḍittha and Ḍavittha" or "the mother of Ḍittha," it is certainly possible to refer to them by the term *pātnīvata* alone.
Therefore, by way of restating a prior action, only a quality (guṇa) is enjoined.
Nor is there an absence of an object to be enjoined;
for that which has already undergone the *pari-agnikaraṇa* rite is itself the object of the injunction, being the referent of the suffix *-kta*.

And since that [fire] is to be enjoined by way of extension (atideśa) as being precisely the archetypal one—according to the principle of the *gṛhamedhīya* butter-portions—and because its requirement is satisfied by that very [fire] due to its established auxiliary efficacy, the subsequent subsidiaries cease by implication through the non-occurrence of the assumption of extension; thus, there is no incidence of the threefold fault (*traidoṣya*).
Furthermore, since the state of having already undergone the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite is impossible if the prior subsidiaries have not been performed, those [prior subsidiaries] are also implied.
Nor does the force of the *kta* suffix imply that [the object] has been cognized by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), such that it would not obstruct the extension of the rule (*atideśa*);

for, as in the case of "with the two threshing-mortars and pestles that have been consecrated" (*prokṣitābhyām ulūkhalamusalābhyām*) and similar instances, there is no obstacle to the fact that even that which is enjoined by this very injunction is expressed by the *kta* suffix, even in the absence of another means of knowledge. // 8 //
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the restatement of the Pātnīvata offering.
(B2) However, the citation of the passage concerning Tvaṣṭṛ is for the purpose of providing knowledge of the counter-positive;
therein lies the determination through inference of the sacrifice, as well as the connections with the chapters, sections, and topical discussions (*adhikaraṇa*).

Since the distinction between ritual acts was established in the preceding section regarding the sentence on the "encircled with fire" (*paryagnikṛta*), he cites the sentence enjoining the previous sacrifice in order to identify its counter-correlate for that distinction: "To Tvaṣṭṛ... (*tvāṣṭram*).

Since the inference of a sacrifice is beyond doubt by means of the previously stated principle—"The [term] *yajati* [denotes a sacrifice] because of its connection with a substance, a fruit, and an enjoyer"—it is said, "having enjoined a sacrifice.
He cites the subject sentence: "paryagnikṛtam" (when the fire has been carried around).

The connection with the context [of the previous section] arises from the investigation into whether that which possesses the characteristic of a deity— specifically when its status as the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is not yet determined— can serve as a differentiator; furthermore, there is an immediate connection by way of a counter-example,

because while it was previously refuted that an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) can convey the status of a deity, here the suffix occurring within an injunction (*vidhi*) is determined to have the deity as its primary referent,
thereby giving rise to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) that an inference of a sacrifice may indeed occur in this case.
Since it is clear [that the objection has been addressed], he states the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself without restating it: "In that case... (*tatra*).

Since that which has two deities cannot be referred to by a term denoting a single deity, the sacrifice intended here is either one modeled after the *pūrvayāga* or one modeled after the *darśapūrṇamāsa*.
As for the statement in the *Vārttika* regarding its being modeled after the *agnīṣomīya*, it is determined to have been made without strict adherence.
Although there exists a context (*prakaraṇa*) that brings the *pūrvayāga* to mind;

Nevertheless, because it is impossible for that [offering] to have both [Agni and Soma] as its deity, it is improper to refer to it by that term; therefore, he establishes that it is a separate ritual action with the words: "of that which has both as its deity."
"Belonging to Agni."

The meaning is that just as in the case of the word *āgneya*, due to the fear of violating the semantic force (*sāmarthya*) [of the compound], there is no inclusion of the *agnīṣomīya* [animal] because of the requirement of the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) produced from the word *agni* alone; so it is here as well.
Furthermore, he shows the necessity of enjoining another sacrifice here because of the absence of any other thing to be enjoined, by stating: "and because of the *paryagnikaraṇa* and so forth."

The word "etc. (ādi) is intended to indicate that [the procedure] is obtained through extension (atideśa) by virtue of being common to other constituent parts; alternatively, it should be understood as serving to include the period of time subsequent to the *paryagnikaraṇa* rite.
This refers to the term "having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa*" (*paryagnikṛta*).

The meaning is that although in the word *paryagnikṛta*—which denotes a substance that has become the object of the rite of circumambulation with fire—the substance, which is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), is enjoined by being extracted [from its compound], it is nevertheless a restatement (*anuvāda*) regarding the aspect of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), because that [qualifier] is already established [by another injunction].

Consequently, since there exists a connection between the substance and the deity—which serves as the basis for inferring a sacrifice—the injunction of a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*) occurs through the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā) of "sacrifice" in the term *utsṛjati*; thus he says: "as a separate ritual act."

Since the word *patnīvat* is a conventional term (*rūḍha*)—like the words *aśvin* and *vājin*—and thus refers to a different deity, it is not possible to enjoin [the offering] there by referring back to the previous sacrifice using the word *utsṛjati*; for that would be obstructed by the fact that the [deity] *iṣṭra* is enjoined as part of the original production (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).
For this very reason, it is not a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).

Nor is it possible for [the action] to occur at a time immediately following the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), because the use of the past-participial suffix (*niṣṭhā-pratyaya*) would entail a figurative interpretation (*lakṣaṇā*), as such a suffix denotes merely the past tense in common with both proximate and remote times. Thus, the particle "only" (*eva*) indicates the exclusion of any other enjoined element.

Therefore, the meaning is that it is logical to enjoin here a distinct ritual action (*karmāntara*) based on a previous sacrifice, by virtue of the commonality of the deity and its attributes (*devatā-guṇa-sāmānya*).

As for the claim made in the *Kaustubha* that the Darśapūrṇamāsa constitute the archetype (*prakṛti*) according to an alternative view, that is intended on the grounds that the term *paryagnikṛta* is common to both the animal sacrifice and the cake-offering (*paśupuroḍāśa*), and thus— when the view is held that the substance is the cake— the similarity of substance is more powerful than the similarity of deity; this does not apply, however, when the reference is to the animal sacrifice itself.

Thus, although it is beyond doubt that the [new] sacrifice has the *pūrvayāga* as its archetype (*prakṛti*) due to similarity with both, the fact that the *Vārttika* mentions the possibility of the *agnīṣomīya* being the archetype by way of an alternative view is clearly stated in the *Nyāyasudhā* to be "without insistence" (*anāsthayā*), because that was intended as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*); for even if the *agnīṣomīya* were the archetype, there would be no contradiction.

(An explanation of how recognition is established even when there are two deities, according to the view of the *Nyāyasudhā* that deityhood resides distributively in the locus of the qualifier-qualified relationship):

However, because Agni and Śuci are construed as deities, and because such [deityhood] functions as a means to the ritual action merely by being the object of reference (*uddeśya*), it is possible for even that which is formless and devoid of qualities to be an object of reference; thus, since the status of being a means to the action would otherwise be untenable, the relation of qualifier and qualified is not apprehended.

Furthermore, if that [mutual relationship] were not accepted, it would result in the repetition of the verb (*ākhyāta*) for each individual [element] in order to express the connection; and since the repetition of the principal verb is utterly improper, and because [otherwise] there would be a separate deity for each, which would entail a distinction of actions (*karmabheda*) necessitating the postulation of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) due to the difference in subordinate qualities, one must conclude that [the elements] are governed by a single action.

Thus, based on the impossibility of this being otherwise, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is understood—so it is written in the *Nyāyasudhā* regarding the *Citrā* section.

Considering the view that, by accepting a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) between two words in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), the subsequent suffix expresses a single deityhood (*devatātva*) that exists collectively (*vyāsajyavṛtti*), he says: "Even in that case," and "of the Manotā."

The meaning is as follows: since the animal victim has Agni-Soma as its deity, the word "Agni" occurring in the mantra "tvam hy agne prathamo manote" denotes both Agni and Soma through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā); similarly here too, it is possible for the word "patnīvat," which is the base of the term "pātnīvata," to denote Tvaṣṭṛ together with the wife [of the gods] through secondary indication.

(Although each [deity] is a separate deity by virtue of the individual secondary derivative suffix, the word *pātnīvata* functions as a restatement (*anuvāda*); the verb *utsṛjati* is a restatement of the abandonment already established by the sense [of the injunction], and thereby the view that it is a restatement of the abandonment of other auxiliary parts is refuted.)
Indicating dissatisfaction with the previous position, he demonstrates the justification for the alternative view by stating "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*):

because, in the absence of a qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), one would have to assume that the suffix following the word expressing the qualifier serves merely for grammatical correctness (*sādhutvamātra*);

therefore, rather than that, it is more appropriate to accept its meaningfulness (*arthavattva*) and [to hold] that the meanings conveyed by those respective suffixes connect with the meanings of their respective bases (*prakṛti*).

Since the distinction between the deities is necessary by means of the difference in words and so forth, even though both deities are first connected to the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), their conjunction in a single action is possible because they are presented within a single sentence; thus, there is no contingency of a split in the ritual act (*karmabheda*). Therefore, even if there is a difference in deity-status (*devatātva*), there is no harm.
This lack of finality is indicated by the phrase "because of hearing the *taddhita* suffix separately" and so on.
"Reiteration."

Even though the act of carrying fire around [the animal] (*paryagnikaraṇa*) is enjoined with reference to the sacrifice by means of the verb *utsṛjati*, the previous sacrifice is brought to mind through the context (*prakaraṇa*). And since that sacrifice is in fact already dedicated to Pātnīvata, the word *pātnīvata* is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*). For this very reason, there is no injunction of a qualified object either. By this, the point stated in the *Āloka*—that when the aforementioned injunction of *paryagnikaraṇa* is made by the verb *utsṛjanti*, the subsequent abandonment of the limbs, which is established by implication, is restated by the verbal root—is refuted.

The meaning is as follows: since it is impossible for the phrase "paryagnikṛtam" (having been encircled by fire) to be construed as the object (*karman*) when [the act] is intended to culminate in the relinquishment of the upper part of the body, and because it is improper to treat it as a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) when it is possible for the meaning of the verbal root to refer to the objective (*uddeśya*), and furthermore because the Vārtika establishes that it is construed precisely as the objective, referring to the relinquishment in the form of abandonment inherent in the sacrifice.

"The repetition [of the injunction] for the sake of a restrictive enumeration (parisaṃkhyā) with respect to the result, like the rule regarding the Ājyabhāga offerings in the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice" refers to the term "Gṛhamedhīya."

Just as in the case of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice, the repeated injunction "he performs the two Ājyabhāga offerings" serves the purpose of exclusion (parisaṅkhyā) by way of its result, so too here the repetition of the injunction regarding the paryagnikaraṇa [is for that same purpose]. Now, one might object: "If there is an annulment of the extended application (atideśa), would it not follow that there is also an exclusion of those auxiliary elements that precede the paryagnikaraṇa? To this, he says: "vṛtte... [meaning: because they have already occurred].
In this case, the quality is not merely the act of carrying fire around [the victim],
but rather, because of the suffix -kta, it is the state of having had the fire carried around, which resides in the animal.
Since that state is impossible if the preceding auxiliary rites have not been performed, the performance of those auxiliary rites is thereby established.

Therefore, the meaning is that there is no defect even in the absence of the word "ending" (*anta*), as in the expression "ending with the *iḍā*. Now, although it is possible for the two *ājyabhāga* offerings—once perceived as things to be performed—to be understood as subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) of the Gṛhamedhīya sacrifice even without another means of knowledge (and thus to constitute an obstacle to the extension of ritual rules, *atideśa*), this is not the case for the "ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*," because its status as being enjoined by another means of knowledge is understood through the suffix *-kta*; since [the rule regarding the ending] depends upon the extension of ritual rules (*atideśa*), [it cannot obstruct it].
He dispels the doubt that "there would be no possibility of its being an obstacle" with the words: "And not... (na ca).

The meaning is that this is justified by the intention [of the text] regarding the time subsequent to the prescription of this rule, because of the perception of its completion. Nor should it be argued: "If this were indeed subject to this prescription, then since there is a reference to the state of having performed the *paryagnikaraṇa* (circumambulation with fire), it would follow that only the *paryagnikaraṇa* itself should be performed"—for in this case, since there is no rule ending with the *paryagnikaraṇa*, the *paryagnikaraṇa* which is obtained through extension (*atideśa*) is such that...

The sense is that the act of carrying fire around the sacrificial animal (*bhūtaparyagnikaraṇa*) is connected [to the *iṣṭi*] because it is of that very same nature; for, by virtue of its prior injunction, it is understood according to what is established, and thus its performance is logically concluded with that [act].
(An examination of the purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections:
Regarding the purpose, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is the performance of a different sacrifice in relation to the *tvaṣṭṛ-yāga*.

However, in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), since it is clear that the sacrifice consists of offering the heart and other limbs of the animal while it is still alive—after performing the ritual acts up to the *paryagnikaraṇa* for the *tvaṣṭṛ-yāga*—to Tvaṣṭṛ and the wives of the gods as deities, it has not been explicitly stated.
Thus ends the eighth section concerning the restatement of the Pātnīvata offering.
(B1) (Section 9 on Adhikaraṇa) (A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 9):
Because he possesses no property, the meditation would be a mere subsidiary to the ritual action. Jaimini 2.3.20:
But because he possesses no property.
Without reference to a specific context, it is heard [in scripture]: "He indeed sacrifices with an oblation by means of an oblation who, having drawn the *adābhya* cup, sacrifices to Soma.
Likewise: "The life-force and breath of him depart who draws the *aṃśu* cup.
Here, the meaning of the first explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) is that Soma is the oblation, he himself is the deity, and he himself is the substance.
"Prāṇa increases the limit of life"—this refers to the second [cup].
In that regard, first of all, the mere act of drawing (grahaṇa) is not enjoined here with respect to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice;
for it is untenable that the drawing, being a form of preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*), should receive the names *Aṃśu* and *Ādābhya*, just as the act of threshing (*avaghāta*) and so forth do not.

If, however, one accepts that those two [words] ending in the accusative case are names of substances to be consecrated (*saṃskārya-dravya*), then—due to the absence of an invariable connection with a sacrifice—it would be impossible to enjoin the taking up of the substance merely by reference to the substance itself.
Therefore, this must be the injunction of a distinct sacrifice qualified by both a substance and a deity;

for by the word *adābhya* there is the designation of the substance known as Soma, which is not subject to injury, and by the word *aṃśu*, the designation of the substance consisting of resinous exudation.
And the second [offering] applies to both cases by the principle of the *saktu* (barley-meal) offering.
As for the deity: in one case it is Soma, and in the other it is Prajāpati, based on the wording of the mantra "To Prajāpati, svāhā!
Furthermore, the root *gṛhṇāti* (to take/grasp) is a restatement (*anuvāda*) in the first instance, but in the second it indicates a sacrifice (*yāga*).

Regarding these two sacrifices, it might be argued that they are subsidiary to the Jyotiṣṭoma on the basis of a passage in the Taittirīya Śākhā belonging to the same class as this one within the context; however, this being the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), we reply: since there is no evidence for the figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of "sacrifice" in the word *gṛhṇāti*, and because in the first sentence the injunction—whose power has been transferred to the quality—indicates that the act of taking (*grahaṇa*) alone is what is to be enjoined, in both cases it is the act of taking itself, designated by the aforementioned name, that is enjoined either as such or as a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for the substance designated by that name.
And thus, even the abandonment of the application of the accusative case is not assumed.
However, since the deity in the form of Soma connects only with the act of "taking" (*grahaṇa*) in the first sentence, it is the taking itself, as qualified by the deity, that is enjoined there.

In the second [sentence], however, the attainment of the deity as a subordinate element of the taking should be understood from the wording of the mantra: "Thou art taken with a support; I take thee, acceptable to Prajāpati."

The *homamantra*, however, is to be understood by taking into account its status as an auxiliary to the sacrifice that occurs later. Furthermore, since there is no contradiction in the fact that the two mentions qualified by the deity are understood—by means of the contextual statement—to be subordinate to the *Jyotiṣṭoma* and to have that [sacrifice] as their object of accomplishment, there is no conflict.

The practical purpose (*prayojana*) in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that, because the sacrifice is subordinate, it falls under the principle of acting according to one's capacity (*yathāśaktinyāya*).
In the established doctrine, it is not so, because [the former] is the primary factor. // 9 //
Thus concludes the ninth section, titled "The State of Not Being Overpowered by Intoxication."
(B2) [The purpose of stating that [the subject] is not to be commenced, its utility for determining the meaning of the first *arthavāda*, and the connection with the preceding chapter and section.]
He cites the subject sentence: "anārabhya" (without reference to a specific context).

The presentation of the fact that [the rite] was taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhītatva*) serves as a proof for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*), in order to refute the reason of the Siddhāntin—who maintains that the connection with the deity is possible through the apprehension of the original sacrifice as a supporting factor—despite its non-existence;
and the refutation of that [prima facie position] will become clear further on.
