If it is asked: "Since the term *agniṣṭoma* is heard [in the text], and the injunction is made as a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that specific sacrifice-form (*saṃsthā*) alone, how can it be said that it is enjoined as a subordinate part of the *jyotiṣṭoma*?"—to this he replies: "And the word *agniṣṭoma*... [and so forth].

In this context, because it is impossible for the term [agniṣṭoma] to denote a *saṃsthā* (concluding form) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the root *yajati* (to sacrifice), and because in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of Bodhāyana and others all the ritual details are prescribed only after designating the Jyotiṣṭoma by the term "Agniṣṭoma," and because its extensive usage is understood to apply to that very sacrifice, it is the Jyotiṣṭoma itself that is denoted by the term "Agniṣṭoma.
By this, the opponent's argument— that there is an injunction for the Agniṣṭoma *saṃsthā*— is refuted.
Therefore, since its nature as a sacrifice is already established, the term *yajati* (he sacrifices) is a restatement for the sake of grammatical correctness;
likewise, the words *atha* and *ataḥ* are also restatements because their meanings are already obtained through the previously mentioned reasoning.

Thus, the meaning is that the piling (*cayana*) is enjoined as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) by means of the preparatory rite (*saṃskāra*) consisting of the installation of the Āhavanīya fire, which serves as the locus, specifically with reference to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.
(An exception is made regarding the fact that the piling [of the altar], even when combined with the performance of the Jyotiṣṭoma, is an auxiliary part of the sacrifice), because it is combined.

The meaning is that [the *sāvitrahoma*] is integrated into the performance of the *jyotiṣṭoma* because it possesses a collection of specific subsidiary elements (*aṅga*)—such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and other rites of the Soma procedure, the *ukhā-saṃbharaṇa*, and the *śikyapratimocana*—which are mixed with the *dīkṣaṇīyā* and so forth;
this is for the purpose of restoring its status as a constituent part of the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatva*).

And this has been stated according to the method established by the author of the *Vidhirasāyana* in his commentary on the thirty-second verse, beginning with "And this [distinction] between the obligatory and the optional... and so forth.

(Now follows the establishment of his own view: that sentences beginning with "atha ata" have the purpose of making known that [the rites] are not subsidiary parts of the sacrifice. In reality, however, while one might assume subsidiariness through the principle of proximity to performance (*anuṣṭhāna-sādeśya*) by postulating successive means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), since the desire-statement (*kāmavākya*) which has already come into operation first makes known that they serve the purpose of fulfilling a specific desire, the sublation of that [subsidiariness to the sacrifice] is what necessarily results; therefore, the position stated in the *Kaustubha*—that these sentences enjoin subsidiariness to the sacrifice as something previously unestablished—is indeed correct.

By this, the argument set forth in the *Vidhirasāyana*—namely, that because fire (*agni*) is stated to be something to be refined (*saṃskārya*) at its production, and because it is stated in the section on the piling (*cayana*) that the Āhavanīya fire is to be placed upon the rice-grains once that [piling] is completed, the status of being a subsidiary to the sacrifice (*kratvaṅgatva*) is attained through the medium of a refinement inseparable from the sacrifice—is refuted. This is because, under the view that the piling of the fire-altar (*agnicayana*) is optional (*kāmya*), the accusative case in the word "fire" (*agnim*) would be abandoned; consequently, since one would have to resort to a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of the fire as a substratum, the fact that the fire is the object of the refinement by the piling would not appear, and thus it would be impossible for the piling to be a subsidiary to the fire.

In the case of a site produced as a byproduct of the optional piling (cayana), even regarding the injunction for the installation of the Āhavanīya fire, since the piling is a subordinate element (aṅga) with respect to the installation of the Āhavanīya that depends on one already employed by another [rite], and because there is no evidence for its being a subordinate element of the sacrifice (kratvaṅga) through that [installation],
it is therefore proper to regard this as an injunction for a subordinate element of the sacrifice that was previously unestablished.

By this, the argument stated by the author of the *Vidhirasāyana* in the thirty-first verse— that when the fire intended for a specific result requires a substratum (*āśraya*), those sentences serve merely to provide the substratum in the form of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and so forth—
is refuted;
for since the act of piling (*cayana*) itself is enjoined as being for the sake of the result, there is no connection with a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), and thus no need for a substratum.
(The author of the *Nyāyasudhā* is refuted by the Commentator [Prakāśakāra] on account of its contradiction with the *Vārttika* on the tenth-book topic concerning the *agni-atigrāhya* offerings, etc.

And here, in the second chapter of the *Saṃkarṣa*, in the section beginning, "The fire-altar (*agni*) is piled up after the *upasad* sacrifice, because it is assisted by the archetype," there is the statement: "For the fire is piled up on the *uttaravedi*. By this, since the fire-altar and the *uttaravedi* have distinct functions, they are to be combined (*samuccaya*).

The prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument states that because the *uttaravedi* is not part of the function (*kārya*) within the *cayana* rite, the properties (*dharma*) of the *uttaravedi* should not be applied there;

however, this is refuted by the established conclusion (siddhānta), which argues that even if there were a combination [of rites], since the function of the *uttaravedi*—namely, the supporting of the fire—is impossible without being a consecration of the fire, and since that function is conceived as one and the same even in the *cayana*, the properties of the *uttaravedi* certainly apply to it due to the unity of the function. Thus it is settled.

In accordance with that, the authors of the *Prakāśa* have thus presented a refutation of the position of simultaneous performance (*samuccaya*)—which had been accepted even in the *Nyāyasudhā*—on the grounds of its contradiction with the statements of the Vārttikakāra regarding the tenth book's section on option (*vikalpa*).

For in the tenth book, in the section concerning the *agni* and *atigrāhya*, the Vārttika refutes the objection that the sentences beginning with "him [one sacrifices] with the *ukthya*" serve as restrictive rules (*niyamārtha*) for the fire-altar (*agni*) which is already obtained through extension (*atideśa*) as an option for the *auttaravedika* altar; it argues that since a purpose is possible in the form of obtaining the proximate results of specific qualities (*guṇakāma*), it is improper for them to have the fruit of restriction which depends upon the more remote process of extension.
Furthermore, since an explicit option between the fire-altar (*agni*) and the high-altar (*uttaravedi*) is stated therein, any contradiction with that is indeed clear.
Even though the statement, "In sacrifices involving a high-altar, one piles [the fire-altar]," appears to be an injunction for their combination, it is not intended as an injunction for combination.

This is because, in the Taittirīya recension, the passage beginning with "Now, therefore, the fire-altar" (*athāto 'gniḥ*) teaches that the fire-altar already produced is to be connected with the sacrifice.
In this context, the term *uttaravedi* is employed because of the desire to understand the specific Soma sacrifice that serves as the subject of the injunction;
even if it were a sentence specifying a particular detail,
it would nevertheless serve the purpose of summarizing that [general rule].

As for the other statement, "For the fire is piled upon the northern altar," because of the word "hi" (for) and the reference to the present tense, that is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) intended as praise for that very [altar].
Therefore, there is indeed an option (*vikalpa*) between the two.
Otherwise, just as the mere fire would not apply [to other rites], even the mere *uttaravedi* altar would not at all apply there in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
[The demonstration that "the fire-altar is built on the Uttaravedi" by refuting the author's view and by showing its consistency with the tenth book of the Jaiminīya-sūtras:
That is incorrect.

Even if the sentence "sottaravedi" (with the high altar) were intended to establish a connection with the sacrifice (*kratu*), since the piling (*cayana*) is integrated into the performance of the Soma sacrifice, it would be possible to determine the specific Soma sacrifice as the objective by the very power of the enjoined piling; consequently, the phrase "sottaravediṣu" would result in being redundant.
Therefore, although there is no other statement in the Taittirīya recension that explicitly establishes a connection with the sacrifice;

Nevertheless, even though this [text] effects the application (*viniyoga*) of the piling (*cayana*) with reference to sacrifices accompanied by the *uttaravedi*, a combination (*samuccaya*) is not difficult to obtain here as well, just as in the case of Agni and Prajāpati, due to the injunction of Prajāpati in conjunction [with the other].

Furthermore, if the phrase "for on the *uttaravedi*" were not injunctive, and if one were to accept an option (*vikalpa*) between the two, then just as there would be an *uttaravedi* independent of the piling, there would likewise result a piling independent of the *uttaravedi*.

Therefore, since its status as an injunction—or at least its capacity to function as an injunction—is necessary for the attainment of the *uttaravedi* as a substratum, it follows that even against one's will, [the combination is established] from that very source.

Intending that the position of conjunction (*samuccaya*) alone is logical—since the establishment of the conjunction of those two follows—he says "And this... in order to justify the attainment of the *uttaravedi* from the tenth book and the statement regarding the option (*vikalpa*).
[He concludes] with the words "because of such statements as... and so forth.

In the sentence concerning the rule for the time of the formal installation (*samāropa*) in the *sattra* sacrifice—namely, "if they are about to pile the fire-altar" (*yady agniṃ ceṣyamāṇā bhavanti*)—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the statement of Kātyāyana, which is an established restatement of an optional alternative.
Therefore, the meaning is that the option concerns the natural state (*svābhāva*) as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*), and not the *uttaravedi* altar as its counter-correlative.
This is because of the aforementioned scriptural statement.
For this statement does not aim to establish the *āhavanīya* fire as a substratum through a continuous connection;

since that [status] is already established by the force of the injunction for the substratum of the piling (*cayana*), it rather—by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*)—directly prescribes the status of being the substratum of the *āhavanīya* in the case where there is no piling. Thus, it is established that the ritual performance consists of the *uttaravedi* alone.

Although, because the direct substratum-hood of that which is enjoined by this injunction is the contextual topic, it is not possible for the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) produced by the piling (*cayana*) to be included as a substratum when that [direct substratum-hood] is already occupied;
nevertheless, since the term *agniṣṭoma* has its primary denotation (*śakti*) in the *Jyotiṣṭoma* itself, there is no sublation [of the rule], as this [term] also lacks any other scope.

For this very reason, in the absence of the [piled] fire, since it is impossible to hold the fire on the *uttaravedi* (which is intended for holding the fire) in the case where the [piled] fire is the locus, it follows by implication that [the rule applies] to the single function of holding the fire.

The meaning is that the statement regarding the option in the tenth [book] is made by taking up a possible alternative; it does not contradict the combination with the *uttaravedi* altar as established by its being the locus for the piling (*cayanādhāra*).

Therefore, in the tenth book—by the text stating that "in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the fire is to be placed either on the *uttaravedi* or on the bare ground"—the option is indeed with respect to the act of placing the fire itself.
(On the view of combination as well, the properties of the *uttaravedi* are applicable to the *citi*).

Nor does it follow that, because the fire-altar (*agni*) and the *uttaravedi* are combined, they would have different functions such that the properties of the *uttaravedi* could not apply to the *citi*; for, by the principle of "separateness of connection" (*saṃyogapṛthaktva*), the *uttaravedi* is understood to have two functions, and its properties are likewise understood to be prompted by those two functions, specifically regarding the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) produced by the piling (*cayana*).

Because it serves the purpose of the specific effect consisting in the direct holding of fire, that portion [of the altar] is subsumed under the function of the *uttaravedi*; thus, the acquisition of its ritual properties (*dharmas*) is logically established.
For this very reason, even in the case of the *uttaravedi* which is combined with another effect consisting in the holding of a leveled mound (*sthaṇḍila*), those properties still apply.
In that regard, when the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*) and the *uttaravedi* are performed together, there is a single performance (*tantratā*) for all non-conflicting elements.
The matter of "reversion" (*āvṛtti*) in cases of contradiction should be examined in the *Kaustubha*.

In reality, however, although there is an option (*vikalpa*) between the fire (*agni*) and the high altar (*uttaravedi*) because they serve the same purpose of maintaining the single fire, the statement of the authors of the *Kalpasūtras* is justified even by the fact that the high altar is desired only occasionally when it happens to be adopted. Therefore, why resort to an option based on their being independent and mutually exclusive (*svatantra-svābhāva-pratiyogitva*)?

Even by that much, since the combination of the two is indeed possible due to the force of the injunction that the *uttaravedi* is the substratum for the piling (*cayana*) and the laying of fire (*adhāna*), it is proper— according to the *Vārttika* as heard— that there be an option (*vikalpa*) with respect to the *uttaravedi*.

(On the meaningfulness of sentences such as "tam ukthyena" [him with the Ukthya] given that the fire-altar is a constituent part of the Jyotiṣṭoma): Now, if the fire-altar is indeed a constituent part of the Jyotiṣṭoma, then since its acquisition would be established through the extension (*atideśa*) of that very sacrifice, sentences such as "tam ukthyena" would be rendered purposeless. To this he replies: "And therefore" (*ataśca*).
The meaning is that by this method—and because the piling (*cayana*) is optional (*vaikalpika*) as the counter-positive of its own absence—[the sentences serve a purpose].

Regarding the statements such as "with the *ukthya*," [the ancient commentators] have criticized the view that they serve both as injunctions for those desiring specific qualities (*guṇakāma*) and as restrictive rules (*niyama*), on the grounds that since their purpose can be fulfilled by the attainment of the proximate qualities about to be mentioned in the tenth book, it is more appropriate to regard them as having the result of restriction based on their being merely optional in relation to the attainment of those various remote extended applications (*atideśa*).

This is because even the purpose of serving those desiring specific qualities depends upon the awareness of its potential futility— which itself depends on the extended application— and thus ultimately depends upon the presentation of that extended application.

Considering that since [the general rule and the specific rule] are equal, when the extended application (atideśa) is present, there is the immediate presence of the optionality (pākṣikatva) indicated by it, and thus it is more appropriate for the restrictive rule (niyama) itself to be the result, he says: "They are for the purpose of restriction" (tanniyamārthāni).
He states that the purpose, consisting in the attainment of desired qualities, is indeed unimpeded: "dependent on the piling" (cayanāśritā).

By the logic of the eighth [book], just as with the carrying forward (*praṇayana*), in order to exclude the worldly piling (*laukika-cayana*) from being the substratum, it is necessary to intend the quality of being for the sake of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) in the act of piling (*cayana*). Even in the absence of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, by the sentence "Now, therefore, the fire" (*athāto 'gnim*), since the Jyotiṣṭoma itself is presented even in the absence of its context, it follows that [the piling] must be for the sake of that which is the means to its *apūrva*.

The meaning is that this will be explained in the tenth book, in the section concerning the *agni* and *atigrāhya*, as follows: since there is no possibility of [the fire-altar] being obtained in its modified form (*vikṛti*) by virtue of becoming its substratum (*āśraya*), the attainment of the qualities desired for those [subsidiaries] based upon it occurs because the fire-piling (*cayana*)—by means of establishing a presentation similar to that of the *jyotiṣṭoma*—attains its status as a substratum through the respective injunctions for the sake of accomplishing the various transcendental results (*apūrva*). Thus, the fruit is the attainment of the qualities desired for those [subsidiaries] which depend upon it.

Therefore, although terms such as *atirātra* denote the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice characterized by those respective forms (*saṃsthās*), it should be understood that because the instruction for the piling of the fire-altar (*cayana*) within the Jyotiṣṭoma is already established by the very statement "Now, therefore, the Fire" (*athāto 'gniḥ*), these terms must refer specifically to the modifications (*vikṛtis*) of those particular forms.
Although it is possible for the *saṃsthās* (termini) to be subordinate to the *cayana* (piling of the altar) because they possess results,

nevertheless, since the attainment of the desire for a specific quality (*guṇakāma*) is possible through the very instruction on the *cayana* connected to the *jyotiṣṭoma* which is the substratum of those *saṃsthās*, their [separate mention] remains entirely redundant.
Thus, Somanātha stated that the words "atirātra" and so forth refer exclusively to the *saṃsthās* themselves and do not indicate the sacrifice (*yāga*).
That [objection] is refuted;
therefore, it should be understood that it is logical that [the text] is intended solely for the modification of those respective forms (*saṃsthā*).
And just as in this case, there is no fault because the intermingling of injunctions (*vidhi*) through two results is accepted elsewhere as well.
Likewise, this should be understood as it has been set forth in the Kaustubha.

(An examination of the purpose of the preceding and subsequent sections: The purpose in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that the *cayana* (piling of the altar), which bears the fruit of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), is to be performed as a distinct sacrifice possessing the characteristics of the *jyotiṣṭoma*; by means of this *cayana*, the *uttaravedi* (northern altar) is set aside.
In the Agniṣṭoma and other such rites, there is only the Uttaravedi;

however, according to the Siddhānta, since it is clear that there is no separate sacrifice in the Agniṣṭoma and that there is an option between the piling of the fire-altar (cayana) and the Uttaravedi, this has not been explicitly stated.
Thus ends the tenth section concerning the fact that the fire-piling is not a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*).

(B1) (11th Topic / [A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 11]) "In a different context, there is a difference in purpose" (Jaimini 2.3.24). In the Kauṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "Having performed the Upasad rites, they offer the Agnihotra for a month; for a month, the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and so forth.

In this regard, since the action—though distant—is brought to mind by the root *juhoti* (to sacrifice) and by terms such as *agnihotra*, there is an injunction of a quality consisting of the month and so forth by way of reference (*anuvāda*) to that action; this is just like [the statement] "one sacrifices in the Āhavanīya fire.

There is no obstacle to enjoining even a non-adoptable element (such as a time) by way of reference to a distant action, provided it is done along with adoptable elements. Furthermore, because the injunction prescribes the performance characterized by multiple qualities such as a plurality of agents and a specific time, there is no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Thus, the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) being that this is not an injunction for a separate action, [the following is stated]: In all cases, the instigating injunction has as its object of activity (*kṛti-viṣaya*)—which is synonymous with "being adopted" (*upādeyatva*)—and, by virtue of its being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it has as its object of knowledge (*prameya*) "being enjoined" (*vidheyatva*), which consists in making known what was previously unknown. Both of these reside in one and the same thing.

The general rule is that [the suffix] functions with respect to both the meaning of the verbal root and the productive activity (*bhāvanā*) by virtue of the direct statement of common designation (*samānābhidhāna-śruti*) and other criteria.

However, when a suitable co-occurring term (*upapada*) is present, it functions with respect to that [term] alone, out of fear of the complexity (*gaurava*) of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭa-vidhi*).

For example, in the case of "one offers in the *āhavanīya* fire," the *āhavanīya* possesses suitability because it serves as the substratum for both being something to be adopted (*upādeya*) and being something to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

For this very reason, in that case, when there is a requirement for a restatement of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), there is somehow a restatement of all *homans*, even those situated far away. In the present case, however, because the month is not something to be enjoined (*anupādeya*), the status of being enjoined must be predicated of the verbal root's meaning itself.

Therefore, since the status of being enjoined also resides in that [root-meaning] by virtue of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is a distinction [between the two cases] because it is impossible to enjoin what has already been enjoined.

Even this being the case, if there were a means of cognition such as proximity (*saṃnidhi*) that serves as a recognizer— as in the case of "he offers [the oblation] in the evening" and so forth— then, having no other recourse, one might resort to a lack of grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), whereby time and the like would be the object of injunction (*vidheya*) and the action would be something to be adopted (*upādeya*) even though it is already established.
But this is not the case.
Nor is it the case that even in the absence of proximity (*sannidhi*) and other factors, the name alone can bring to mind a prior action; for,

by the word *juhoti* in the sentence "He offers the Agnihotra," there arises a presentation of the sacrifice characterized by its being a distinct type of sacrifice (*vijātīya-homatva*), and it is logical that this very same presentation— brought about by proximity and causing the *juhoti* of the sentence "He offers in the evening" to also have as its object its own specific domain— should be understood in that way.
That [name] acts as an obstacle to the understanding that the meaning [of the word] is subordinate to the action.

However, names such as "Agnihotra" are capable of producing a cognition in which the sacrifice is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) and its being a sacrifice to the deity Agni is the qualifier (*prakāra*).
For there is no evidence that the ritual previously [performed] was necessarily one to the deity Agni.
Because the homa-ness of a different class is not presented by the name; otherwise, it would result in the impossibility of using them together as synonyms;

because the avoidance of over-extension was established in the *Udbhid* section precisely by the absence of prior usage [of the term for other things]; and because the acceptance of both etymological derivation (*yoga*) and conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is not admitted.

Otherwise, even for the sake of avoiding the over-extension resulting from the fear of having to resort to possessive indication (*matvarthalakṣaṇā*) and the like, if one were to accept conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), that same consequence would apply to *soma* and other such terms as well;
therefore, there is no presentation of the object by means of the name alone.

For this very reason, in cases where only the name is heard in connection with a non-enjoinable quality (*anupādeyaguṇa*), and not the verbal root—as in "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [is performed] for the sake of all"—[the action is understood through the name].

In that case, since it would follow that the name itself is to be enjoined by virtue of its coreferentiality with the object (artha) which is to be adopted, there is no separate ritual action (*karmāntara*) because that [enjoinability] is obstructed by the mental presentation produced by the name.
Alternatively, let it be granted that there is no separate ritual action because that sentence belongs to the same context (*prakaraṇika*).

Therefore, in the present instance, since it is impossible for the name to obstruct the fact that the meaning of the root *juhoti* is what is to be enjoined, the status of being a separate ritual action is established through "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*), which consists in the non-presentation of a ritual already known as being connected with non-adoptable qualities.

In this context, the function (*vyāpāra*) consists in the connection with a non-adoptable quality (*anupādeyaguṇa*), which—by way of removing adoptability from its own locus—results, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), in the induction of adoptability residing in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*).
It is that [connection] which, because it is not present [in the root-meaning], does not obstruct its being prescribed (*vidheyatva*) through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with adoptability.

Therefore, one should note that it is not merely the "connection with a non-adoptable quality" as stated by the ancients that serves as the purpose, but rather the "absence of any general adoptable quality."
Therefore, it is established that this is indeed the injunction of a distinct ritual action qualified by time.

Similarly, in the case of "On the southern bank of the Sarasvatī, [there is] an offering to Agni on eight potsherds," the location— which is an irreducible factor— is likewise [distinct], because the term *āgneya* (related to Agni) is common [to other rites] and thus lacks the capacity to bring to mind a previously known ritual action.
Regarding the occasion (*nimitta*), however, there is the case: "Having resolved (*āgūrya*) to perform a *satra* sacrifice, one should sacrifice with the *viśvajit*.
Here, *āgūraṇa* means the mental resolve (*saṃkalpa*).
This *viśvajit* sacrifice is for one who does not subsequently perform that *satra*.
From the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Viśvajit," [it follows that] this is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).
Nor can there be the origination (*utpatti*) of that which has already been enjoined or employed by this [injunction];
for there is no evidence to sublate an origination understood through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the injunction and so forth, in the absence of proximity (*sannidhi*). // 11 //
Thus ends the eleventh section concerning other topics (*prakaraṇāntarādhikaraṇa*). (The summary of the subject passages and the connection by way of remainder, etc., have been stated.
Thus it is heard in scripture.

The phrase "one should sacrifice for a month with the Vaiśvadeva, for a month with the Varuṇapraghāsas, for a month with the Sākamedha, and for a month with the Śunāsīrīya" includes these sentences together with their respective connective particles (*anuṣaṅga*) by means of the first word [of each].

Since there is no connection to the context of subordinate elements (*guṇaprakaraṇa-saṅgati*) through the examination of other means of proof, the author does not explicitly state the connection based on elimination (*pāriśeṣikī saṅgati*) because it is obvious; instead, he states the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) itself, beginning with the word "In that case" (*tatra*).
(Conclusion of the prima facie argument regarding the absence of a division of ritual acts:
Because there is no subverting evidence.

The meaning is that even though it is impossible to enjoin [the time] in the form of being accomplished by an action (kṛtisādhyatva)—just as one cannot enjoin the agent and so forth—it is possible for it to be enjoined as the locus of the action (kṛtyadhikaraṇatva), etc., just like the time of the full moon (paurṇamāsī) and so forth; thus, there is no subverting factor consisting in its being unfit for injunction.

Nor can it be argued that because of the presence of a subverting factor in the form of the exclusion by the contextual times of evening and so forth, the inclusion of a quality such as "month" would be untenable, resulting in a distinction based on that quality;

for there is no contradiction, since the relationship between the earlier and later times of evening and morning can be established through a relation of pervader and pervaded (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva), just as in the case of the times of the new moon (amāvāsyā) and the afternoon.
Nor does the contradiction with continuity—implied by the word "month" ending in the accusative case, which denotes absolute conjunction—constitute a subverting factor;

for when an inevitable obstruction arises due to the necessity of attending to food, movement, and so forth, it is appropriate, as in the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the *jāteṣṭi* sacrifice, that the contextual time-period be accommodated.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the occasion known as "living."

In the Siddhānta, since there is no contradiction because a limitation by means of a month is possible— just as it is by means of the evening and morning times— and because the inclusion of the month is appropriate only in the case of an optional (kāmya) performance;
furthermore, the lack of support from the context (prakaraṇa) of the Kauṇḍapāyina-sattra does not constitute a sublation.

Either by way of a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) for the *agnihotra* and other rites— which were excluded from the state of being initiated (*dīkṣita*) for the Kauṇḍapāyinas— prescribing their performance for one month; or else, even though the time of one month is prescribed with reference to the *agnihotra* and other rites,

because the application of the year-long *satra* sacrifice cannot be completed by the six-month *soma* sacrifices, there arises a requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) on the part of the *agnihotra* and other rites which, having been presented as the objects of reference (*uddeśya*), remain expectant despite being otherwise self-sufficient.
The sense is that its support is established either by the statement of the application (*prayoga-vacana*) of the subsidiaries (*sattra*) or by its injunction with respect to the fruit (*phala*).

Thus, when other subverting arguments have been refuted as indicated by the phrase "due to the absence of subverting arguments," there remains a subverting argument consisting in the contingency of a split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*)—which would result in the introduction of multiple distinct factors—adduced by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). This occurs because, while restating the *prāptakarman* (the rite already established), one would simultaneously enjoin the sequence of the *upasad*s following it, the month-long duration, and the plurality of agents; this [subversion] would lead to a division based on the qualities (*guṇakṛtabheda*).
He refutes [the objection] separately, out of a sense that it must be respected as establishing his own tenet, with the words: "In the case of a plurality of agents... and so forth.

In passages such as "for a month [one should sacrifice] with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," since it does not pervade [all cases] due to the absence of multiple qualities, the prima facie view concludes that this cannot establish a distinct ritual action. To this, he states the final position (*siddhānta*), demonstrating that although a distinction cannot be established by other means of proof, it is necessary to explain the nature of "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) in order to prove distinction through that very context; thus, he says: "Therefore... [the proposition that there is a difference of ritual actions due to a different context]. Even when a distinction is impossible through other authorities, he explains the essential nature of "difference of context" because it is required to establish distinction on that basis, and thereby sets forth the final conclusion.
"Everywhere"—this means in all cases.

By the phrase "by direct statement and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the direct statement of the words that establish the occurrence [of the action] within the meaning of the verbal root.
He states an exception to the general rule: "yogyeti" (in the case of one who is fit).
(Since the Āhavanīya fire is something to be employed, there is a difference in ritual acts based on the sentence concerning the Āhavanīya; this is what is meant by "fitness.")

The point is this: although the Āhavanīya fire—being established by the injunction for its installation (*ādhāna*)—is not made known by this [present] injunction as being the object of the injunctive operation known as "to be taken up" (*upādeyatva*) or "to be enjoined" (*vidheyatva*);

nevertheless, according to the method stated in the *Kaustubha* regarding the section on the Vājapeya sacrifice, since it is the object of that [injunction] in the form of being qualified by the act of making manifest (*prāduṣkaraṇa*) and so forth for the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), there is no contradiction with that [earlier injunction].
Therefore... [the phrase ends with "ata eveti"].

The meaning is that, precisely because it is necessary for the object denoted by the secondary word (*upapada*) alone to be the thing enjoined, out of fear of the resulting burden of enjoining a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭavidhi*).

Even though there is no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to present the specific injunctions that would normally provide those [details], the *juhoti* itself presents them as a restatement (*anuvāda*), which is indicated in some way by the word "somehow" (*kathaṃcit*).

Although it is impossible for time and so forth to be "to-be-adopted" (*upādeya*) in the sense of being pervaded by the agent's effort (*kṛti*), they can still be enjoined in the sense of being the locus of effort (*kṛtyadhikaraṇatva*), etc.; and in the case of the ritual action (*karman*), there is both "to-be-adopted" status in the sense of being pervaded by the person's effort and the status of being enjoined.
Therefore, the meaning is that because time and so forth come into contact with the injunction, their status as auxiliary elements to the intended meaning is established.
(An objection regarding the name’s capacity to bring the *homa* to mind even in the present context:

Having restated the objection— that because the name, which is stronger than even the *prakaraṇa* (context), exists as a means of bringing [the action] to mind, it is logical that it prevents the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between being the thing to be taken up (*upādeyatva*) and being the thing to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*), and thus the establishment of a difference [between actions] cannot occur— he refutes it:
And not so.
"Of what kind? [is the question].

[The phrase] "because it is impossible for a noun, which generates a cognition qualified by gender and number, to bring about the presentation of such a verbal root-meaning, [the noun] does not constitute an obstacle to the status of the verbal root-meaning as the thing to be enjoined" means: [the noun] does not [qualify it] because it is not connected with gender and number. This is because, at the stage when the meaning of the partial sentence consisting of the noun is understood, the noun brings about a cognition of its own meaning qualified by gender and number; therefore, the status of being the thing to be enjoined—which resides in the verbal root-meaning understood from the verbal root-word—is not qualified by those [gender and number].
Because there is an absence of identical mode of presentation (*samānaprakāratva*), it is impossible for [the verbal root] to be restricted by the name.
For when it is established that the verbal root refers to a previously encountered object of proximity, its status as expressing a thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*) is obstructed.

Consequently, by virtue of proximity, [the root] does not connect with gender or number in the case of that which is understood from the word *juhoti* occurring in the sentence "He offers the Agnihotra" (*agnihotraṃ juhoti*).

In that case, since the specific *homaviśeṣa* (particular sacrifice) presented as a qualifier is established by the word "juhoti" within the sentence "sāyaṃ juhoti" (he offers in the evening), it is logical that it acts as an obstacle to the status of being the object to be enjoined (*vidheya*) by that same "juhoti.

However, in the present instance, the [sacrifice] presented by the name [Agnihotra] is presented as having the property of being a particular *homa* that is connected with gender and number, and thus it is not obstructed from being the object to be enjoined by the "juhoti" occurring in the *māsāgnihotra* sentence.

Intending to show the difference [between the two cases] by considering that, because it is impossible to cause [the name] to be understood [in that way], there is no possibility of the name being an obstacle to the meaning of the predicate residing in it, he says: "But as for names such as 'Agnihotra'..."
"No."

The meaning is as follows: since the status of being a *homa* whose deity is Agni is denoted by the term *agnihotra*, and since that [status] remains uncontradicted even in a previously unknown *homa*, its application to that term is possible; therefore, there is no evidence for the presentation of a previously established ritual action alone.

He dispels the objection that if the capacity [to denote the ritual] were based on being a *homa* of a different class (*vijātīya*), it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), by stating "over-extension" (*atiprasaṅga*).

Granted that the name indeed generates a cognition characterized by the mode of being a *homa* of a different class; otherwise, it would be impossible for the name to function as an extended application (*atideśaka*) through secondary metaphor (*gauṇa*) in the case of the Māsāgnihotra.

Nevertheless, the point is that the presentation of that [different class]—by way of the rule of extended application through a name—is conducive to differentiation (*bheda*), and thus does not constitute an obstacle to its being a thing to be enjoined (*vidheya*).

Since the statement "The Darśapūrṇamāsa [rites] for all" is taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), there is a distinction of rites by virtue of the name; however, if it were part of the context (*prākaraṇika*), there would be no distinction of rites—thus, it is not a separate rite.
The meaning is that there is merely a connection of the fruit with the two objects presented by their names, through the ellipsis of unstated words denoting what must be performed.

And this point was stated by Bhavadeva regarding these two sentences, having accepted that they are taught as unconnected (anārabhyādhīta); he asserted that the name itself acts as the restrictive factor due to the absence of any other proximate obstructing factor.

In reality, however, in the sūtra—"The desire for all [fruits] [is accomplished] through the optional subsidiaries by virtue of the context (prakaraṇa)," etc.—it is stated that this is indeed due to the context.

Therefore, even though there is coreferentiality with the verb (ākhyāta-sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the name, proximity (sannidhi)—as in the case of "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—can be asserted as the obstructing factor; thus, the fact that it is not a separate ritual action is easily established.
He states another alternative: "or eight."
(An examination of how a name brings to mind a ritual action even in a context where there is no *prakaraṇa*, as in the *vividiṣā* passage:

For this very reason—in the *vividiṣā* passage, where there is no *prakaraṇa*—the previously mentioned [passage] states: "But he is a sacrificer of the self who knows: 'By this, this limb is consecrated; here, this limb is placed by this. Here, by means of the pronoun *etad* (this), which refers back to what was stated before...
Regarding the phrase "he who should sacrifice," that which is indicated by the word *yat*—which has an established meaning—in the previously mentioned scripture, refers to the prior rites.
In that context, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb, it is indeed accepted that the name [of the rite] brings to mind the prior rites.

One who, having understood that "by this rite this limb of mine is refined, my sins are destroyed, and I am endowed and augmented by merit," performs the rite, is an *ātmayājī* (self-sacrificer) sacrificing for the sake of self-purification.

And the meaning of the Śatapatha-śruti passage—"He who sacrifices to the gods for the sake of desire is superior"—is as follows. He concludes the established doctrine [siddhānta] with the words "ataḥ" (therefore), which means "for this very reason."

(The non-presentation qualified by the absence of a non-adoptable quality is not what constitutes a different context [prakaraṇāntara], but rather the non-presentation qualified by the absence of the general property of being an adoptable quality.

For this reason, the function of a non-adoptable quality is merely to bring about the status of being an adoptable quality residing in the meaning of the verbal root; and that [function] is possible both when a non-adoptable quality exists and when there is an absence of the general property of being an adoptable quality—this is the meaning.

And thus, the intention is that the presentation of "difference of context" (*prakaraṇāntara*) as a means of proof is appropriate in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the status of a separate rite for the sentence occurring in the *Gṛhamedhīya* section: "In the tenth [day], he performs the two *ājyabhāga* offerings."
(Distinction between Repetition and the Principle of a Different Context, despite the overlap of their substrata):

Nor should it be argued—"In this way, even in cases such as *tanūnapātaṃ yajati*, since there is an absence of common qualities among the things to be enjoined (*upādeya*), difference would result from the principle of a different context alone; what then is the use of repetition? This should not be said, because although there is an overlap of the substrata, the nature of the principles themselves does not overlap.

Setting aside the notion of acceptability (*upādeyatā*) through repetition (*abhyāsa*), the function (*vyāpāra*) consists precisely in bringing about the status of being something to be enjoined (*vidheyatva*) within the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) by means of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*).
For this very reason, in that case, proximity (*sannidhi*) is what is obstructed, but it is not an absolute obstacle as it is in the case of a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*).
In a different context, however, there is no function of bringing about the status of being enjoined through elimination.
Since there is no such impossibility when time and so forth are accepted as being objects of injunction by way of a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*),

rather, even though there is another object of injunction, the verbal root-meaning itself is made an object of injunction in order to achieve co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the quality of being something to be undertaken (*upādeyatā*), such as sleep and the like; therefore, because the body of the logical principle (*nyāyaśarīra*) remains unmixed, the distinction [of the action] from a different context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is appropriate— this detailed explanation should be seen in the *Kaustubha*.

(Regarding the scope of the *prakaraṇāntara* principle [the rule of a different context], even in cases such as "for a month, by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices," there is an injunction for a set of six sacrifices.

Likewise, even where there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a verb in a different context—as in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, within the sections on the New and Full Moon sacrifices and the Four-Monthly sacrifices, in the passage: "On this night, he offers the Agnihotra with barley-gruel"—it is the same.

In that case, since the principle of *prakaraṇāntara* (a different context) is impossible—because it consists in the absence of the commonality of qualities to be adopted—the distinction [of the action] does not arise; therefore, one must conclude that by necessity, the name itself is what brings about the remote [action].

Similarly, in the passage "for a month, with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," according to the seventh-book principle (*sāptamika-nyāya*), the words *darśa* and *pūrṇamāsa* extend the application (*atideśa*) of the properties such as the materials and deities belonging to the three archetypal (*prākṛta*) sacrifices.

And because these are understood as being combined through their inclusion in a single compound, [the properties] such as the materials and deities—which are understood from the originative injunction (*utpattivākya*) to be combined—are [to be applied] to each individual [sacrifice].

Because it is impossible for [the number] to be enjoined as part of the action, just like the number [of sacrifices], one must conclude that there is a difference in the actions; therefore, six sacrifices must be enjoined, just as in the case of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

As for what is stated in the *Bālaprakāśa*—that the distinction between two groups of three is established by the number two assisted by a different context—that is incorrect, as seen in the *Kaustubha*. This is because the dual number is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) pertaining to two groups, and thus, just as the plural number in the phrase "He offers the *samits*" does not effect a distinction, the dual number here cannot be a differentiator.

(Just as in the case of the connection with time, so too in the case of the connection with place and the connection with a cause, there is a difference of ritual acts because the prior act cannot be brought to mind in the absence of its presence. Among the five non-optional factors—consisting of time, place, cause, fruit, and the object to be refined—it has been established that when there is a connection with the non-optional factor of time, it constitutes a different ritual act; he now extends this [principle] to the connections with place and cause by saying "in the same way."

Although the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is not explicitly heard here, nevertheless, because the connection between the material (*dravya*) and the deity (*devatā*) would otherwise be untenable, a sacrifice is inferred; thus, the meaning is that this is a distinct ritual act from the archetypal *Āgneya* sacrifice.
The phrase "of that which is non-qualifiable" (*anupādeyasya*) is to be understood as having an example following it.
The same should be understood regarding the phrase "of the sign" (*nimittasya tu*) as well.

One might raise the objection that, just as in the case of "the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices] for all," because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the verb, the previous rite is brought to mind by the name *Āgneya*, and thus, as in that case, no distinction (*bheda*) is established; in order to refute this doubt, he says:
"of the word *Āgneya*."

The meaning is that because the word *āgneya* is not a name (*nāmadheya*), it—like the root *yaji*—denotes merely any substance having Agni as its deity, regardless of whether the action has been previously enjoined or not; thus, it lacks the capacity to necessarily bring to mind a specific prior action in the absence of proximity (*sannidhi*).

The meaning is that while there may be a sublation of its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with [the term *sannidhi*] in cases such as the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices when *sannidhi* exists, it is not logical for that sublation to occur in its absence.
(The sūtra *phalaṃ cākarmasaṃnidhau* [Jaimini 2.3.25] is for the purpose of removing further doubts regarding the subject of the fruit; this is the illustration concerning place and occasion.

Although, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the subsequent sūtra *phalaṃ cākarmasaṃnidhau*, it is possible to include both place and occasion—just as the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) is included—it is precisely there that these examples are demonstrated.
It is appropriate to act [in this way];
nevertheless, since it is already known here that these two, like Time, serve as the means for accomplishing other actions, they are presented here.
As for the subsequent sūtra, however, its purpose is to remove further doubts regarding the results and so forth; thus, there is no fault.
The purpose has not been stated because it is obvious.
Thus ends the eleventh section, concerning other topics.
(B1) (12th Adhikaraṇa / [A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 12]) And the fruit.
"One desiring splendor should offer an eight-potherd cake sacred to Agni"—this refers to the fruit [of the action].
But regarding the preparatory rite, "he sprinkles the Audumbarī post" is a distinct act from the sprinkling of the rice-grains;
thus, there are exactly five [factors] that are not to be taken up as objects of desire.
Likewise, this has been explained in detail in the Kaustubha under the section concerning the Vājapeya sacrifice. // 12 //
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the result as that which is to be refined.
(B2) [The purpose of the present section stated by way of resolving a further doubt:

Since it was established in the preceding section that [the difference of context] is a differentiator through the non-proximity indicated by the word *prakaraṇāntara* in the sūtra— by means of establishing that what has been stated in the previous section is to be enjoined as something to be adopted through its co-referentiality with the "remainder" (*pāriśeṣya*)— this [non-proximity] can only occur when there is a connection with qualities that are not to be adopted (*anupādeya-guṇa-yoga*).

Since the fruit (*phala*) and the object to be refined (*saṃskārya*) cannot be connected [with the action], and since being an auxiliary (*aṅgatva*)—which is synonymous with being the object of an application injunction (*viniyoga-vidhi*)—resides in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), it follows by implication that it implies "prescriptiveness" (*vidheyatva*), which is synonymous with being the object of an originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*). However, because this does not imply "acceptability" (*upādeyatva*), such a connection is impossible; therefore, there is no differentiation [of the ritual] by way of a separate context (*prakaraṇāntara*). On the other hand, time, place, occasion (*nimitta*), and so forth, serve as qualifiers of the performance (*prayoga*) precisely because they cause the performance, and thus they possess "acceptability," which is synonymous with being brought about by the performance of the meaning of the verbal root.

In order to dispel the specific doubt that it is appropriate for [the word] to function as a differentiator by way of that [quality], he cites the subject sentence in a separate topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) under this sūtra, beginning with "phalasya" (of the fruit).

By the use of the term "of the fruit" (*phalasya*) as if it were already established, the author indicates that, according to the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), this section is intended as an elaboration (*prapañca*) of the preceding topic (*pūrvādhikaraṇa*).

For this very reason, there is no excessive regard for the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). (This concludes the demonstration that the sentences concerning desire for radiance and so forth do not constitute separate rituals.)
"Desire for trees."
*Ruk* means radiance.

Here too, as in the case of the *deśavākya*, since it is impossible to enjoin a fruit for a previously existing sacrifice by postulating a sacrifice inferred from the connection between a substance and a deity, the action must be enjoined; therefore, the meaning is that it is a distinct ritual (*karmāntara*) in relation to the original *Āgneya* sacrifice.
(This is the indication of another example.)
(And the removal of the previously mentioned excessive doubt:

As for that which was cited by the ancients—the sentence occurring within the context of the Aśvamedha, "The *traidhātavī* becomes the *dīkṣaṇīyā*"—because of the difference between the *traidhātavī* and the *dīkṣaṇīyā*, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is untenable; therefore, [the term] is secondary (*jaghanya*).

In the section on the *dīkṣaṇīyā* [offering], having accepted the definition of the function of the *dīkṣaṇīyā* as a consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), it was shown that because the sacrificer—who is the object of the consecration—is brought to mind, there is no presentation of [the sacrificer] as being endowed with non-prescribed qualities; thus, due to "another context" (*prakaraṇāntara*)—in the form of the absence of such a presentation—the rite is a distinct action (*karmāntara*) compared to the *traidhātavī* sacrifice, which is prescribed for the sake of a well-known independent fruit.

However, that illustration regarding the object of consecration is untenable, because the name *traidhātavī*, like the expression "the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices for all," is not in grammatical apposition with the verbal root and therefore logically serves to bring the previously mentioned rite to mind.

Indicating with the word "tu" that [the opponent's view] is incorrect because there is no evidence for it being a separate action, [the author] sets that aside and cites another example: "But as for the object to be refined... (saṃskāryasya tu).

In this regard, although both [the fire and the fuel] possess the status of being the primary factor (*aṅgin*), since the quality of being an instigator of performance also exists [in the fire] by virtue of its being the object of desire and so forth, it necessarily implies that which is to be adopted (*upādeya*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the removal of the specific doubt—that a separate injunction of a distinct action (*karmāntaravidhi*) is required to obtain the status of being the thing enjoined (*vidheya*) as co-referential with that [fire]—is achieved.
(The refutation of the Bālaprakāśa view that singularity is not something to be adopted):

Here, the authors of the *Prakāśa* state: "In the *Bālaprakāśa*, having accepted that 'being the object of an action' (*kṛtiviṣayatva*) constitutes 'being something to be adopted' (*upādeyatva*), they argue that by the mere absence of this [objectivity], just as in the case of time and so forth, the universal of 'singularity'—which qualifies the agent—as well as the universal of 'Brāhmaṇahood' and others, are likewise not things to be adopted.

For this very reason, the verse in the *Śāstradīpikā* belonging to the section on the *Pratipadādhikaraṇa* is consistent: 'The singularity of the sacrificer is not something to be adopted, just like time. Thus it was said.
He states the refutation of that [position] as a consequence: "Just as... (yathā).

The refutation of that [position] should be seen here in the Kaustubha. As for the purpose: in the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), because it is the archetype (prakṛti), the rite is performed on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad); however, in the final conclusion (siddhānta), as in other modified rites (vikṛti), it is performed on the full or new moon day (parvan). This has not been stated here because it is self-evident.
Thus ends the twelfth section concerning the fruit as that which is to be refined.
(B1) (Thirteenth Topic / [A.2 Pāda 3 Adhikaraṇa 13]) In proximity.
There are counter-examples for all five types of non-adoptable [injunctions] when they occur in proximity.

In the context of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, there are four such cases: “One should sacrifice on every full moon day,” “One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* on level ground,” “One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives,” and “One who desires heaven should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*.”
With reference to the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, [the text states]: “He performs the *sviṣṭakṛt* from the remnant.

Here, in all such cases, because proximity prevents the status of being a subordinate element (*vidheya*) within its own sphere for that which is to be refined as a remnant, the injunction—out of parsimony—is understood to authorize merely the prescription of the performance characterized by time and place for an action already established, but it does not enjoin the very origination (*utpatti*) of the action itself.
But where the performance is also already established— as in "he who [performs] the *iṣṭi*," and so forth—
there, by way of restating the established performance, there is an injunction solely for the time and other such factors.

For even though it is impossible for place and time to be things to be directly undertaken (*upādeya*), an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) is possible insofar as they are subordinate members of the sacrifice.

In the case of a conditional occasion (*nimitta*), however, since it is impossible for the condition and its consequence to stand in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgitva*) to one another, it will be explained that even though the rite is already established, there is an injunction of application (*viniyoga-vidhi*) which assigns the rite— already obtained— to the purpose of destroying sin, as inferred from its connection with the condition. But in the cases of a result (*phala*) or a sanctification (*saṃskārya*), the injunction of application which assigns the already established rite to those [results or sanctifications] as its objectives is quite clear.
Therefore, even when there is proximity and the presence of non-essential qualities, it does not constitute a different ritual action. // 13 //
Thus ends the thirteenth section, concerning the counter-example of another topic.

(B2) (Counter-examples for all five things that are not to be adopted): Intending that the word "fruit" (*phala*) in the Sūtra serves as an indicator for all things that are not to be adopted, he says: "of all five," and "inferred from the connection with the cause" (*nimitta*).

The meaning is that, because the indicative mark (nimitta) compels performance by necessitating the practical application (prayoga), and since that application requires a result, its application is for the purpose of destroying sin, according to the method to be explained in the section concerning "as long as one lives" (yāvajjīvādhikaraṇa).
This is indeed clear.
The meaning is that since those two serve the purpose of the person, it is clear that the application of the ritual action is for its own sake alone.
The other [passages] have clear meanings.

Thus, just as the proximity known as *adhikāra* (qualification) serves as a proof for the status of a statement as a reference (*anuvāda*) to an existing rite— and thereby acts as an obstacle to the establishment of a separate rite— so too, even in its absence, wherever there is a perception of a reference to an existing rite through the use of words such as *yat*, one should understand that it likewise acts as an obstacle; for in such cases, the assignment of time is made precisely to the rite already present and established,
as in the passage beginning with "He who [performs] the *iṣṭi*," and so forth.

Or, as in the case of such passages as "In the sacrifices equal to the Punarādheya, one performs the Agnihotra," there is no difference between the [original] sacrifice and the Agnihotra; for even though the word *yat* (which marks an injunction) is absent from the Agnihotra sentence, it is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the Agnihotra injunction, serving to indicate that the purpose of the injunction is merely to prescribe the limit (the *udavasānīyā* sacrifice) required by the prohibition "The initiated one does not perform the Agnihotra. This is how it should be understood.

In this regard, the definition of the nature of proximity—which acts as an obstacle to the valid cognition of difference—and non-proximity—which generates the valid cognition of difference—is to be found in the Kaustubha;
it is not stated here for fear of prolixity.
Thus ends the thirteenth section, concerning the counter-example of another topic.
(B1) (Section 14 / [Chapter 2, Pāda 3, Adhikaraṇa 13] The Āgneya [offering]).

Having established that the Agneya sacrifice is connected with two points of time, based on the scriptural text: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is offered at the new moon," this [subsequent statement] is an injunction of a different ritual action from the Agneya which is joined with those two times;
for the distinction [of the actions] is established either by the difference of context (*prakaraṇāntara*) or by repetition (*abhyāsa*).

The injunction of the full moon day (*paurṇamāsī*) alone by the other [text] for that which is already prescribed by this [text] must be rejected, because it is precluded by the time [of performance] enjoined at the origin (*utpatti-śiṣṭa*).

Nor should it be argued that there is a dual prescription of the very same rite by two injunctions—on account of its being "crowned with prosperity" (*abhyudayaśiraskatā*)—in the manner of the specific substance [denoted] by the words *piṅgākṣī* and *ekahāyanī*;
for when a single [substance] presented by both the words *piṅgākṣī* and *ekahāyanī* is enjoined by a single injunction, there is no sublation (*bādhaka*).
In the present case, however, since an injunction prescribed by one [text] cannot be the object of an injunction by another, it must be a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).

Therefore, when it is argued that the performance of two *Āgneya* offerings on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*) is the purpose of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), we reply: because this [injunction] is a subordinate part (*śeṣa*) of the single *Aindrāgna* injunction, it does not possess independent injunctive force. Furthermore, the praise of the *Aindrāgna* offering is achieved through its association with the praiseworthy *Āgneya*.
Therefore, it is not a separate action. // 14 // 47 //
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the purpose of praising Agni.
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Bhāṭṭadīpikā composed by the venerable Khaṇḍadeva.
(B2) "In two times" means:
The meaning is: by means of the sentence, "The cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is not displaced [from its place] on the new-moon day and the full-moon day.

In the *Paurṇamāsī-adhikaraṇa*, following the method stated by the author of the *Prakāśa* in the *Prakaraṇāntara-adhikaraṇa*, the difference between the two *Āgneya* offerings is set aside on the grounds that they constitute a single ritual action. However, the author of the *Nyāyasudhā* has demonstrated that there is indeed a difference between the two *Āgneyas* due to their connection with two distinct qualities—the full-moon day and the new-moon day—which cannot coexist within a single ritual action.

Because it was prepared by oneself, the singular number in the word "āgneyam" (belonging to Agni) is technically improper; however, it is used with the intention of expressing the genus (*jāti*), thus intending the singular number.
This is what is meant by "it is heard [in scripture]."
The meaning is "in another section";
that is, because of a different context.
By this, the immediate connection based on extended application (*atideśika*) is indicated.

Intending to show that the distinction [of the ritual] from another context (*prakaraṇāntara*) is not established because proximity (*sannidhi*) somehow acts as an obstacle, he sets forth the differentiator even while that [proximity] exists: "Or because of repetition" (*abhyāsād vā*).

Although, according to the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view, there is no possibility of performing two *āgneya* offerings simultaneously because they share the same deity, nevertheless, the simultaneous performance is set aside precisely because it would render the restatement (*punarvidhi*) purposeless. Alternatively, he says "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), intending that the performance of two *āgneyas* follows from the preparation of two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*).

Since the statement "that which belongs to Agni" (yad āgneyaḥ) determines through another sentence that the *āgneya* cake has Agni alone as its deity, one might ask how it can serve as a praise for the *aindrāgna* cake; in response to this expectation, he says: "It is praised."

The meaning is that, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is praise of the *aindrāgna* [offering] by way of its association with the praised *āgneya*, because the excellence of the *āgneya* is understood from the injunction accompanied by the explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) beginning with, “Indeed, the Aṅgirases went from here to the heavenly world as the last. The practical application (*prayojana*) of this is that, on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), two *āṣṭākapāla* [cakes] belonging to the two *āgneya* offerings would be performed due to their connection therewith;
however, this is not the case in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). This has not been stated explicitly as it is clear.
Thus ends the fourteenth section concerning the purpose of praising Agni.
Thus ends the third pāda of the second adhyāya in the Bhāṭṭadīpikāprabhāvalī.
